chapters.title: Dedication
paragraphs: MOST HONORABLE, MAGNIFICENT AND SOVEREIGN LORDS, I am convinced that only a virtuous citizen can offer his country honors it is able to accept. For thirty years I have worked to make myself worthy of paying you some public tribute. This fortunate occasion makes up in some measure for the insufficiency of my efforts, and so I have thought myself entitled to follow the promptings of the zeal that inspires me, rather than the right that ought to have authorized me. I had the happiness to be born among you. How could I reflect on the equality nature has ordained between men, and on the inequality they have introduced, without thinking of the profound wisdom by which, in this State, the two are happily combined and made to coincide? They coincide in the way that best conforms to natural law and best serves society, the maintenance of public order and the happiness of individuals. I have searched for the best rules common sense can lay down for the constitution of a government, and I have been so struck to find all of them already in practice in yours that, even had I not been born within your walls, I should have thought it indispensable to offer this picture of human society to your people. Of all peoples, yours seems to me to possess its greatest advantages and to have best guarded against its abuses.

If I had been able to choose the place of my birth, I should have preferred a society whose size was proportioned to the limits of the human faculties, that is, to the possibility of being well governed. In it every person would be equal to his occupation, so that no one would be obliged to hand over to others the functions entrusted to him. It would be a State in which all the individuals knew one another well, so that neither the secret machinations of vice nor the modesty of virtue could escape the notice and judgment of the public. And the pleasant custom of seeing and knowing one another would make the love of country a love of the citizens rather than of the soil.

I should have wished to be born in a country where the interest of the Sovereign and that of the people were necessarily one and the same, so that all the movements of the machine would tend always toward the general happiness. This could not be so unless the Sovereign and the people were one and the same person. It follows that I should have wished to be born under a democratic government, wisely tempered.

I should have wished to live and die free. By this I mean that I should be subject to the laws in such a way that neither I nor anybody else could throw off their honorable yoke. It is an easy and salutary yoke, and the haughtiest necks bear it all the more meekly because they are made to bear no other.

I should therefore have wished that no one within the State could claim to be above the law, and that no one outside it could dictate terms the State would be obliged to recognize. For whatever the constitution of a government may be, if a single man within its jurisdiction is not subject to the law, all the rest are necessarily at his discretion. And if there is a national ruler within and a foreign ruler without, then however they may divide their authority, it is impossible for both to be duly obeyed, or for the State to be well governed.

I should not have chosen to live in a republic of recent founding, however excellent its laws. I should have feared that the government, perhaps framed differently from what the circumstances of the moment required, might not suit the new citizens, or they might not suit it, and that the State would risk overthrow and destruction almost as soon as it came into being. For liberty is like those solid and succulent foods, or those generous wines, that nourish and strengthen robust constitutions used to them, but ruin and intoxicate weak and delicate constitutions not suited to them. Peoples once accustomed to masters are unable to do without them. If they try to shake off the yoke, they only estrange themselves further from freedom. They mistake for freedom an unbridled license that is its exact opposite, and almost always, through their revolutions, they deliver themselves to seducers who make their chains heavier than before. The Roman people itself, a model for all free peoples, was wholly incapable of governing itself when it escaped the oppression of the Tarquins. It had been debased by slavery and by the ignominious tasks imposed on it, and at first it was no better than a stupid mob, which had to be controlled and governed with the greatest wisdom. Only so could it grow accustomed, by degrees, to breathe the health-giving air of liberty, and its minds, enervated or rather brutalized under tyranny, might gradually acquire that severity of morals and spirit of fortitude which would finally make it the most respectable of all peoples. I should, then, have looked for a peaceful and happy Republic as my country, one of such antiquity that it was lost, as it were, in the night of time. It would have suffered only such shocks as served to show and strengthen the courage and patriotism of its subjects. Its citizens, long accustomed to a wise independence, would have been not only free but worthy to be so.

I should have wished to choose a country that a fortunate impotence had turned away from the brutal love of conquest, and that a still more fortunate situation secured against the fear of itself being conquered by other States. It would be a free city situated among several nations, none of which had any interest in attacking it, while each had an interest in preventing the others from doing so. In short, it would be a Republic with nothing to tempt the ambition of its neighbors, which could reasonably count on their assistance in case of need. It follows that a republican State so happily situated would have nothing to fear but itself. If its members trained themselves in the use of arms, it would be to keep alive the military ardor and courageous spirit that suit free men so well and sustain their taste for liberty, rather than from any need to provide for their defense.

I should have sought a country in which the right of legislation belonged to all the citizens, for who can judge better than they under what conditions they should live together in the same society? I should not have approved of Plebiscita like those of the Romans, in which the rulers of the State, and those most interested in its preservation, were excluded from the deliberations on which its security often depended. By the most absurd inconsistency, the magistrates in those assemblies were deprived of rights that the meanest citizens enjoyed.

On the contrary, I should have wished, in order to prevent self-interested and ill-conceived projects and all such dangerous innovations as finally ruined the Athenians, that no man be free to propose new laws at pleasure. This right should belong exclusively to the magistrates, and even they should use it with so much caution, the people should be so reserved in giving their consent, and the promulgation of such laws should be attended with so much solemnity, that there would be time enough, before the constitution could be upset by them, for everyone to be convinced of three things. First, it is above all the great antiquity of the laws that makes them sacred and venerable. Second, men soon learn to despise laws they see altered every day. Third, States that accustom themselves to neglect their ancient customs under the pretext of improvement often bring in greater evils than those they try to remove.

I should have been especially careful to avoid, as necessarily ill-governed, a Republic whose people imagined themselves able to do without magistrates, or at least to leave them only a precarious authority, and so imprudently kept for themselves the administration of civil affairs and the execution of their own laws. Such must have been the rude constitution of the primitive governments that emerged directly from a state of nature. This was another of the vices that contributed to the downfall of the Republic of Athens.

I should rather have chosen a community in which the individuals were content to sanction their laws, and to decide the most important public affairs in general assembly on the motion of the rulers. They would have set up honored tribunals, carefully distinguished the several departments, and each year elected some of the most capable and upright of their fellow-citizens to administer justice and govern the State. In such a community the virtue of the magistrates would bear witness to the wisdom of the people, and each class would do the other honor. Suppose that in such a case some fatal misunderstanding arose to disturb the public peace. Even these intervals of blindness and error would bear the marks of moderation, mutual esteem and a common respect for the laws, which are sure signs and pledges of a reconciliation as lasting as it was sincere. Such are the advantages, most honorable, magnificent and sovereign lords, that I should have sought in the country where I should have chosen to be born. And if providence had added to all these a delightful situation, a temperate climate, a fertile soil and the most beautiful countryside under Heaven, I should have desired only one thing to complete my felicity: the peaceful enjoyment of all these blessings in the bosom of this happy country. I should have lived at peace in the sweet society of my fellow-citizens, practicing toward them, after their own example, the duties of friendship, humanity and every other virtue. And I should have left behind me the honorable memory of a good man and of an upright and virtuous patriot.

But suppose I were less fortunate, or had grown wise too late, and saw myself reduced to ending an infirm and languishing life in other climates. I should be vainly regretting the peaceful repose I had forfeited through the imprudence of youth. Even so, I should at least have kept the same feelings in my heart, though denied the opportunity to use them in my native country. Filled with a tender and disinterested love for my distant fellow-citizens, I should have addressed them from my heart in terms much like these.

"My dear fellow-citizens, or rather my brothers, since ties of blood as well as the laws unite almost all of us, it pleases me that I cannot think of you without thinking at the same time of all the blessings you enjoy. None of you, perhaps, feels the value of them more deeply than I, who have lost them. The more I reflect on your civil and political condition, the less I can conceive that the nature of human affairs could admit of a better. In all other governments, when the question is how to secure the greatest good of the State, nothing gets beyond projects and ideas, or at best bare possibilities. But as for you, your happiness is complete, and you have nothing to do but enjoy it. To be made perfectly happy you need only learn to be satisfied with being so. Your sovereignty was acquired or recovered by the sword, and has been maintained for two centuries by your valor and wisdom. It is at length fully and universally acknowledged. Honorable treaties have fixed your boundaries, confirmed your rights and secured your repose. Your constitution is excellent, dictated by the profoundest wisdom and guaranteed by great and friendly powers. Your State enjoys perfect tranquillity. You have neither wars nor conquerors to fear. You have no other master than the wise laws you have made yourselves, and these are administered by upright magistrates of your own choosing. You are not so wealthy as to be enervated by effeminacy, and so to lose, in the pursuit of frivolous pleasures, the taste for real happiness and solid virtue. Nor are you so poor as to need more assistance from abroad than your own industry can procure. In the meantime the precious privilege of liberty, which great nations maintain only by submitting to the most exorbitant impositions, costs you hardly anything to preserve.

May a Republic so wisely and happily constituted last for ever, as an example to other nations and for the felicity of its own citizens! This is the only prayer you have left to make, the only precaution that remains to be taken. For the future it depends on yourselves alone (not to make you happy, for your ancestors have saved you that trouble), but to make that happiness lasting, by your wisdom in enjoying it. Your preservation depends on your constant union, your obedience to the laws and your respect for their ministers. If the smallest trace of bitterness or distrust remains among you, hasten to destroy it, as an accursed leaven that sooner or later must bring misfortune and ruin on the State. I conjure you all to look into your hearts and to hearken to the secret voice of conscience. Can any of you find, throughout the universe, a more upright, more enlightened and more honorable body than your magistracy? Do not all its members set you an example of moderation, of simplicity of manners, of respect for the laws and of the most sincere harmony? Place, therefore, without reserve, that salutary confidence in such wise superiors which reason ever owes to virtue. Consider that they are your own choice, that they justify that choice, and that the honors due to those you have dignified are necessarily yours by reflection. Not one of you is so ignorant as not to know that when the laws lose their force, and those who defend them lose their authority, security and liberty are universally impossible. Why, then, should you hesitate to do cheerfully and with just confidence what your true interest, your duty and reason itself would have bound you to do all along?

Never let a culpable and pernicious indifference to the maintenance of the constitution lead you to neglect, in case of need, the prudent advice of the most enlightened and zealous of your fellow-citizens. Let equity, moderation and firmness of resolution continue to govern all your proceedings, and show the whole universe the example of a valiant and modest people, equally jealous of their honor and of their liberty. Beware especially, as the last piece of advice I shall give you, of sinister constructions and venomous rumors, whose secret motives are often more dangerous than the actions they are aimed at. A good and trusty watch-dog barks only at the approach of thieves, and a whole house will wake and heed the first alarm he gives. But we hate the importunity of those noisy curs that are perpetually disturbing the public repose. Their continual ill-timed warnings keep us from attending to them even when they may perhaps be necessary."

And you, most honorable and magnificent lords, the worthy and revered magistrates of a free people, permit me to offer you in particular my duty and homage. If there is a station in the world that can confer honor on those who fill it, it is undoubtedly the one that virtue and talents combine to bestow, the one you have made yourselves worthy of and to which your fellow-citizens have raised you. Their worth adds a new luster to your own. You have been chosen, by men capable of governing others, to govern themselves, and so I cannot but hold you as much superior to all other magistrates as a free people, and particularly the one over which you have the honor to preside, is superior by its wisdom and its reason to the populace of other States.

Permit me to cite an example of which there ought to have existed better records, and one that will always be near to my heart. I cannot recall, without the sweetest emotions, the memory of that virtuous citizen to whom I owe my being, and by whom I was often instructed, in my infancy, in the respect that is due to you. I see him still, living by the work of his hands and feeding his soul on the sublimest truths. I see the works of Tacitus, Plutarch and Grotius lying before him among the tools of his trade. At his side stands his dear son, receiving, alas with too little profit, the tender instructions of the best of fathers. But if the follies of youth made me for a while forget his wise lessons, I have at length the happiness of knowing that, whatever one's propensity to vice, an education mingled with love is not easily thrown away entirely.

Such, my most honorable and magnificent lords, are the citizens, and even the common inhabitants, of the State you govern. They are those intelligent and sensible men of whom, under the name of workmen and the people, other nations usually hold a low and false opinion. My father, I own with pleasure, was in no way distinguished among his fellow-citizens. He was only such as they all are. And yet, such as he was, there is no country in which men of the highest character would not have coveted his acquaintance, and cultivated it even to their advantage. It would not become me, nor is it, thank Heaven, at all necessary, to remind you of the regard such men have a right to expect from their magistrates. They are equal to the magistrates by education and by the rights of nature and birth, and inferior only by their own will, in the preference they owe to your merit; and for granting you that preference they can claim some sort of acknowledgment on your side. I understand with lively satisfaction that in all your behavior toward them the greatest candor and condescension accompany the gravity that becomes the ministers of the law, and that you so well repay, by your esteem and attention, the respect and obedience they owe you. This conduct is not only just but prudent, since it happily tends to blot out the memory of many unhappy events that ought to be buried in eternal oblivion. It is also the more judicious because it tends to make this generous and equitable people find pleasure in their duty. It makes them naturally love to do you honor, and it causes those who are most zealous in maintaining their own rights to be at the same time the most disposed to respect yours.

It ought not to be thought surprising that the rulers of a civil society should have the welfare and glory of their communities at heart. But it is uncommonly fortunate for the peace of men when those who look upon themselves as the magistrates, or rather the masters, of a more holy and sublime country show some love for the earthly country that maintains them. I am happy to have it in my power to make so singular an exception in our favor, and to rank among its best citizens those zealous depositaries of the sacred articles of faith established by the laws, those venerable shepherds of souls. Their powerful and captivating eloquence is all the better suited to carry the maxims of the gospel to men's hearts because they are themselves the first to put them into practice. All the world knows how successfully the art of the pulpit is cultivated at Geneva. But men are so used to hearing divines preach one thing and practice another that few have a chance of knowing how far the spirit of Christianity, holiness of manners, severity toward themselves and indulgence toward their neighbors prevail throughout the whole body of our ministers. It is perhaps given to the city of Geneva alone to produce the edifying example of so perfect a union between its clergy and men of letters. It is in great measure on their wisdom, their known moderation and their zeal for the prosperity of the State that I build my hopes of its perpetual tranquillity. At the same time I notice, with a pleasure mingled with surprise and veneration, how much they detest the frightful maxims of those accursed and barbarous men of whom history gives us more than one example. In order to support the pretended rights of God, that is to say their own interests, these men have been less greedy of human blood in proportion as they were more hopeful that their own in particular would always be respected.

I must not forget that precious half of the Republic which makes the happiness of the other, and whose sweetness and prudence preserve its tranquillity and virtue. Amiable and virtuous daughters of Geneva, it will always be the lot of your sex to govern ours. Happy are we, so long as your chaste influence, exercised solely within the limits of conjugal union, is used only for the glory of the State and the happiness of the public. It was thus that the female sex commanded at Sparta, and thus you deserve to command at Geneva. What man can be such a barbarian as to resist the voice of honor and reason when it comes from the lips of an affectionate wife? Who would not despise the vanities of luxury on seeing your simple and modest attire, which, from the luster it takes from you, seems the most favorable to beauty? It is your task to perpetuate, by your insinuating influence and your innocent and amiable rule, a respect for the laws of the State and harmony among the citizens. It is yours to reunite divided families by happy marriages. Above all, it is yours to correct, by the persuasive sweetness of your lessons and the modest graces of your conversation, those extravagances our young people pick up in other countries. From those countries, instead of the many useful things by which they might profit, they bring home hardly anything but a puerile air and a ridiculous manner, acquired among loose women, together with an admiration for I know not what so-called grandeur, and paltry recompenses for being slaves, which can never come near the real greatness of liberty. Continue, therefore, always to be what you are, the chaste guardians of our morals and the sweet security for our peace. On every occasion, exert the privileges of the heart and of nature in the interests of duty and virtue.

I flatter myself that I shall never be proved mistaken in building on such a foundation my hopes of the general happiness of the citizens and the glory of the Republic. It must be confessed, however, that with all these advantages it will not shine with that luster by which the eyes of most men are dazzled. A puerile and fatal taste for such luster is the most mortal enemy of happiness and liberty.

Let our dissolute youth seek elsewhere light pleasures and long repentances. Let our pretenders to taste admire elsewhere the grandeur of palaces, the beauty of carriages, sumptuous furniture, the pomp of public entertainments and all the refinements of luxury and effeminacy. Geneva boasts nothing but men. Such a sight has nevertheless a value of its own, and those who have a taste for it are well worth the admirers of all the rest.

Deign, most honorable, magnificent and sovereign lords, to receive, with equal goodness, this respectful testimony of the interest I take in your common prosperity. And if I have been so unhappy as to be guilty of any indiscreet transport in this glowing effusion of my heart, I beseech you to pardon me, and to attribute it to the tender affection of a true patriot and to the ardent and legitimate zeal of a man who can imagine no greater felicity for himself than to see you happy.
Most honorable, magnificent and sovereign lords, I am, with the most profound respect,
Your most humble and obedient servant and fellow-citizen.
J. J. ROUSSEAU. Chambéry, June 12, 1754.

chapters.title: Preface
paragraphs: Of all the human sciences, the most useful and the least complete seems to me to be the science of mankind. I will venture to say that the single inscription on the Temple of Delphi holds a precept more difficult and more important than all the huge volumes the moralists have ever written. I regard the subject of this discourse as one of the most interesting questions philosophy can pose. Unhappily for us, it is also one of the thorniest that philosophers can be asked to solve. For how are we to know the source of inequality between men if we do not first know mankind? And how can man hope to see himself as nature made him, through all the changes that time and place must have worked in his original constitution? How can he tell what is fundamental in his nature from what his circumstances, and the advances he has made, have added or altered in his primitive condition? Consider the statue of Glaucus, so disfigured by time, seas and tempests that it looked more like a wild beast than a god. The human soul has been altered in society in much the same way. A thousand causes recurring without end have changed it: the gaining of a multitude of truths and errors, changes in the constitution of the body, and the constant clash of the passions. So, to speak figuratively, it has changed in appearance until it is hardly recognizable. We no longer find a being that acts always from fixed and invariable principles, or that celestial and majestic simplicity its divine Author impressed upon it. We find only the frightful contrast of passion mistaking itself for reason, and of understanding grown delirious.

It is still more cruel that every advance of the human species carries it farther from its primitive state. The more discoveries we make, therefore, the more we deprive ourselves of the means of making the most important discovery of all. Thus, in one sense, it is by our very study of man that knowledge of him is placed beyond our power.

It is easy to see that we must look for the origin of the differences that now distinguish men in these successive changes in the constitution of man. It is allowed that men are naturally as equal among themselves as the animals of every kind were, before physical causes introduced the varieties we now observe in some of them.

In fact, it cannot be supposed that these first changes, however they arose, altered every individual of the species all at once and in the same manner. It is natural to think that the condition of some grew better or worse, and that they acquired various good or bad qualities not inherent in their nature, while others remained longer in their original condition. Such, doubtless, was the first source of the inequality of mankind. It is much easier to point this out in general terms than to assign it with precision to its actual causes.

Let my readers not imagine, then, that I flatter myself with having seen what seems to me so difficult to discover. I have entered here upon certain arguments and risked some conjectures. I did so less in the hope of solving the difficulty than in order to throw some light on it and reduce the question to its proper form. Others may easily go farther along the same road, yet no one will find it very easy to reach the end. For it is by no means a light undertaking to distinguish properly what is original from what is artificial in the actual nature of man. It is no lighter to form a true idea of a state that no longer exists, perhaps never did exist, and probably never will exist; and yet we must have true ideas of it if we are to judge our present state properly. It takes more philosophy than can be imagined to enable anyone to determine exactly what precautions he should take to make solid observations on this subject. It seems to me that a good solution of the following problem would not be unworthy of the Aristotles and Plinys of our age. What experiments would have to be made to discover the natural man? And how are those experiments to be made in a state of society?

I am so far from undertaking to solve this problem that I think I have considered the subject enough to venture to declare in advance something else. Our greatest philosophers would not be too good to direct such experiments, nor our most powerful sovereigns to carry them out. We have very little reason to expect such a combination, especially one joined with the perseverance, or rather the succession of intelligence and good will, that success would require on both sides.

These investigations are so difficult to make, and have so far been so little thought of. Yet they are the only means left to us of removing a multitude of difficulties that keep us from knowing the real foundations of human society. It is our ignorance of the nature of man that casts so much uncertainty and obscurity on the true definition of natural right. For, says Burlamaqui, the idea of right, and more particularly that of natural right, are ideas manifestly relative to the nature of man. It is therefore from this very nature, he goes on, from the constitution and state of man, that we must deduce the first principles of this science.

We cannot see without surprise and disgust how little agreement there is among the authors who have treated this great subject. Among the more important writers there are scarcely two of the same mind. I say nothing of the ancient philosophers, who seem to have done their best to contradict one another on the most fundamental principles. The Roman jurists subjected man and the other animals indiscriminately to the same natural law, because they took that name to mean the law that nature imposes on herself rather than the law she prescribes to others. Or rather, it was because of the particular sense the term law has among those jurists, who seem on this occasion to have understood by it only the general relations nature establishes between all animated beings for their common preservation. The moderns understand by the term law merely a rule prescribed to a moral being, that is to say, to a being who is intelligent and free and is considered in his relations to other beings. They therefore confine the jurisdiction of natural law to man, as the only animal endowed with reason. But each defines this law after his own fashion, and they have founded it on such metaphysical principles that very few among us can understand them, much less discover them for ourselves. So the definitions of these learned men, which differ in everything else, agree only in this: it is impossible to understand the law of nature, and consequently to obey it, without being a very subtle casuist and a profound metaphysician. All of which is as much as to say that mankind, in establishing society, must have used a capacity that is acquired only with great difficulty, and by very few persons, even in a state of society.

We know so little of nature, and agree so poorly about the meaning of the word law, that it would be difficult to settle on a good definition of natural law. Thus all the definitions we find in books have, apart from their lack of uniformity, another fault. They are drawn from many kinds of knowledge that men do not possess naturally, and from advantages they can have no idea of until they have already departed from that state. Modern writers begin by asking what rules it would be expedient for men to agree on for their common interest. Then they give the name of natural law to a collection of these rules, with no other proof than the good that would result if everyone practiced them. This is undoubtedly a simple way of making definitions, and of explaining the nature of things by almost arbitrary conveniences.

But as long as we are ignorant of the natural man, it is vain to try to determine either the law originally prescribed to him or the law best suited to his constitution. We can know only one thing with any certainty about this law. If it is to be a law, those it binds must be aware of their submission to it. And if it is to be natural, it must come directly from the voice of nature.

I therefore set aside all those scientific books, which teach us only to see men as they have made themselves. I contemplate the first and simplest operations of the human soul, and I think I can perceive in it two principles prior to reason. One of them interests us deeply in our own welfare and preservation. The other excites a natural repugnance at seeing any other sensible being, and particularly any of our own species, suffer pain or death. It is from the agreement and combination that the understanding is able to establish between these two principles, without any need to bring in that of sociability, that all the rules of natural right appear to me to be derived—rules that our reason is afterwards obliged to establish on other foundations, when its successive developments have led it to suppress nature itself.

If we proceed in this way, we shall not be obliged to make man a philosopher before he is a man. His duties toward others are not dictated to him only by the later lessons of wisdom. So long as he does not resist the internal impulse of compassion, he will never hurt any other man, nor even any sentient being. The exception is those lawful occasions when his own preservation is concerned and he is obliged to give himself the preference. By this method we also put an end to the old disputes over whether animals share in natural law. It is clear that, lacking intelligence and liberty, they cannot recognize that law. But they partake in some measure of our nature, because of the sensibility they are endowed with. They ought therefore to partake of natural rights, so that mankind is subject to a kind of obligation even toward the brutes. It appears, in fact, that if I am bound to do no injury to my fellow creatures, this is less because they are rational than because they are sentient beings. And since this quality is common to men and beasts, it ought to entitle the latter at least to the privilege of not being wantonly ill-treated by the former.

Besides, the study of the original man, of his real wants and of the fundamental principles of his duty, is the only proper method we can adopt to remove all the difficulties presented by the origin of moral inequality. The same study bears on the true foundations of the body politic, on the reciprocal rights of its members, and on many other similar topics, equally important and obscure.

Look at human society with a calm and disinterested eye, and at first it seems to show us only the violence of the powerful and the oppression of the weak. The mind is shocked at the cruelty of the one, or moved to lament the blindness of the other. Nothing in life is less permanent than those external relations, which accident produces more often than wisdom, and which we call weakness or power, riches or poverty. So all human institutions seem at first glance to be founded merely on banks of shifting sand. Only by taking a closer look, and removing the dust and sand around the edifice, do we perceive the immovable basis on which it is raised and learn to respect its foundations. Now, without a serious study of man, of his natural faculties and their successive development, we shall never be able to make these necessary distinctions. We shall never be able to separate, in the actual constitution of things, what is the effect of the divine will from what human art has innovated. The political and moral investigations to which the question before us leads are therefore useful in every respect, and the hypothetical history of governments is an equally instructive lesson for mankind.

In considering what we should have become, had we been left to ourselves, we should learn to bless Him whose gracious hand corrected our institutions and gave them an immovable basis. He has prevented the disorders that would otherwise have arisen from them, and has made our happiness come from the very sources that seemed likely to plunge us into misery.
Quem te deus esse Jussit, et humanâ quâ parte locatus es in re, Disce. Persius, Satire iii, 71.
A DISSERTATION
ON THE ORIGIN AND FOUNDATION OF THE INEQUALITY OF MANKIND

It is of man that I have to speak. The question I am investigating shows me that I must address myself to men, for those who are afraid to honor truth do not ask questions of this sort. I shall therefore uphold the cause of humanity with confidence before the wise men who invite me to do so. I shall not be dissatisfied if I acquit myself in a manner worthy of my subject and of my judges.

I conceive that there are two kinds of inequality among the human species. One I call natural or physical, because nature establishes it, and it consists in differences of age, health, bodily strength, and the qualities of the mind or of the soul. The other may be called moral or political inequality, because it depends on a kind of convention and is established, or at least authorized, by the consent of men. This second kind consists of the different privileges that some men enjoy to the prejudice of others. Such are being richer, more honored, more powerful, or even in a position to exact obedience.

It is useless to ask what the source of natural inequality is, because the simple definition of the word answers that question. It is still more useless to ask whether there is any essential connection between the two inequalities. That would be only to ask, in other words, whether those who command are necessarily better than those who obey. It would be to ask whether strength of body or of mind, wisdom or virtue, are always found in particular individuals in proportion to their power or wealth. Slaves might perhaps discuss such a question in the hearing of their masters, but it is highly unbecoming to reasonable and free men in search of the truth.

The subject of this discourse, then, is more precisely the following. I mean to mark, in the progress of things, the moment at which right took the place of violence and nature became subject to law. I mean to explain by what sequence of miracles the strong came to submit to serve the weak, and the people to purchase imaginary repose at the expense of real felicity.

The philosophers who have inquired into the foundations of society have all felt the need to go back to a state of nature, but not one of them has got there. Some have not hesitated to credit man, in such a state, with the idea of just and unjust. They never trouble to show that he must have had such an idea, or that it could have been of any use to him. Others have spoken of the natural right of every man to keep what belongs to him, without explaining what they meant by belongs. Others again began by giving the strong authority over the weak, and went straight on to the birth of government. They gave no thought to the time that must have passed before the words authority and government could have had any meaning among men. In short, every one of them, dwelling constantly on wants, avidity, oppression, desires and pride, has transferred to the state of nature ideas that were acquired in society. In speaking of the savage, they described the social man. It has not even occurred to most of our writers to doubt whether the state of nature ever existed. Yet it is clear from the Holy Scriptures that the first man received his understanding and commandments directly from God, and so was not himself in such a state. And if we give the writings of Moses the credit that every Christian philosopher ought to give them, we must deny that men were ever in the pure state of nature, even before the deluge. The only exception would be if they fell back into it through some very extraordinary circumstance. That is a paradox it would be very embarrassing to defend and quite impossible to prove.

Let us begin, then, by setting facts aside, since they do not affect the question. The investigations we may enter into on this subject must not be taken for historical truths. They are only conditional and hypothetical reasonings, better suited to explaining the nature of things than to establishing their actual origin. They are like the hypotheses our physicists form every day about the formation of the world. Religion commands us to believe that God Himself took men out of a state of nature immediately after the creation, and that they are unequal only because it is His will that they should be so. But it does not forbid us to form conjectures, based solely on the nature of man and the beings around him, about what might have become of the human race had it been left to itself. This, then, is the question put to me, and the one I propose to discuss in this discourse. My subject interests mankind in general, so I shall try to use a style suited to all nations. Or rather, forgetting time and place, I shall attend only to the men I am speaking to. I shall suppose myself in the Lyceum of Athens, repeating the lessons of my masters, with Plato and Xenocrates for judges and the whole human race for audience.

O man, of whatever country you are, and whatever your opinions may be, behold your history, as I have thought to read it. I read it not in books written by your fellow creatures, who are liars, but in nature, which never lies. All that comes from her will be true. You will meet with nothing false, unless I have involuntarily put in something of my own. The times I am going to speak of are very remote. How much you have changed from what you once were! It is, so to speak, the life of your species that I am going to write, drawing on the qualities you have received. Your education and habits may have depraved those qualities, but cannot have entirely destroyed them. There is, I feel, an age at which the individual man would wish to stop. You are about to inquire after the age at which you would have liked your whole species to stand still. You are discontented with your present state, for reasons that threaten your unfortunate descendants with still greater discontent. So perhaps you will wish it were in your power to go back. And this feeling should be a panegyric on your first ancestors, a criticism of your contemporaries, and a terror to the unfortunates who will come after you.

chapters.title: Part 1
paragraphs: To judge rightly of the natural state of man, it may be important to consider him from his origin and to examine him, as it were, in the embryo of his species. Yet I shall not trace his organization through its successive developments, nor stop to ask what his animal system must have been at the beginning, before it became what it now is. I shall not ask whether his long nails were at first, as Aristotle supposes, only crooked talons. I shall not ask whether his whole body was covered with hair, like a bear's, or whether walking on all fours, with his eyes turned toward the earth and confined to a horizon of a few paces, did not at once mark out the nature and limits of his ideas. On this subject I could form only vague and almost imaginary conjectures. Comparative anatomy has made too little progress so far, and the observations of naturalists are too uncertain, to give an adequate basis for any solid reasoning. So I shall set aside the supernatural information we have on this point, and pay no attention to the changes that must have taken place in man's internal and external structure as he put his limbs to new uses and fed himself on new kinds of food. I shall suppose his structure to have been at all times what it appears to us today: that he always walked on two legs, used his hands as we do, turned his eyes over all of nature, and measured the vast expanse of Heaven with his gaze.

Suppose we strip this being, so constituted, of all the supernatural gifts he may have received and of all the artificial faculties he can have acquired only through a long process. Suppose we consider him, in a word, just as he must have come from the hands of nature. We then see an animal weaker than some and less agile than others, but, taking him all round, the most advantageously organized of any. I see him satisfy his hunger at the first oak and quench his thirst at the first brook. I see him find his bed at the foot of the tree that gave him his meal, and with that, all his wants are supplied.

The earth was left to its natural fertility and covered with immense forests, whose trees were never mutilated by the axe. In such a state it would offer food and shelter on every side to every species of animal. Men, scattered among the other animals, would observe and imitate their industry, and so rise even to the instinct of the beasts. They would have this advantage: every species of brutes was confined to one particular instinct, whereas man, who perhaps has none peculiar to himself, would take over them all. He would live on most of the different foods that the other animals shared among themselves, and so would find his subsistence much more easily than any of them.

From infancy men would be used to the harshness of the weather and the rigor of the seasons. They would be inured to fatigue, and forced, naked and unarmed, to defend themselves and their prey against other ferocious animals, or to escape them by flight. In this way men would acquire a robust and almost unalterable constitution. Children would be born with their parents' excellent constitution and would strengthen it by the very exercises that first produced it, and so they would gain all the vigor the human frame is capable of. In this case nature treats them exactly as Sparta treated the children of her citizens. She makes strong and robust those who come well formed into the world, and she destroys all the rest. In this she differs from our modern communities, in which the State makes children a burden to their parents and so kills them indiscriminately before they are born.

The body of a savage man is the only instrument he understands, and he uses it for various purposes that ours, for lack of practice, cannot serve. Our industry deprives us of the force and agility that necessity obliges him to acquire. If he had had an axe, could he have broken so large a branch from a tree with his bare arm? If he had had a sling, could he have thrown a stone with so great a velocity? If he had had a ladder, would he have climbed a tree so nimbly? If he had had a horse, would he himself have been so swift of foot? Give civilized man time to gather all his machines about him, and he will no doubt easily beat the savage. But if you want to see a still more unequal contest, set them against each other naked and unarmed. You will soon see the advantage of having all one's forces constantly at one's disposal, of being always prepared for every event, and of carrying oneself, as it were, perpetually whole and entire about with one.

Hobbes contends that man is naturally intrepid and intent only on attacking and fighting. Another illustrious philosopher holds the opposite. Cumberland and Puffendorf also affirm that nothing is more timid and fearful than man in the state of nature, and that he is always trembling and ready to flee at the least noise or the slightest movement. This may be true of things he does not know. I do not doubt that he is terrified by every novelty that presents itself, when he does not know the physical good or evil he may expect from it and cannot compare his own strength with the dangers he is about to meet. Such circumstances, however, rarely occur in a state of nature, where all things proceed in a uniform manner and the face of the earth is not subject to the sudden and continual changes that arise from the passions and caprices of men living together in bodies. But savage man lives dispersed among the other animals, and soon finds himself in a situation to measure his strength against theirs, and soon compares himself with them. He perceives that he surpasses them more in adroitness than they surpass him in strength, and he learns to be no longer afraid of them. Set a bear or a wolf against a robust, agile and resolute savage, as they all are, armed with stones and a good cudgel. You will see that the danger will be at least on both sides, and that after a few trials of this kind, wild beasts, which are not fond of attacking one another, will be very unready to attack man, having found him to be as wild and ferocious as themselves. As for animals that really have more strength than man has adroitness, he is in the same situation as all the weaker animals, which nevertheless are still able to subsist. He has this one advantage besides: he is equally swift of foot, and he finds an almost certain refuge in every tree, so he is at liberty to take it or leave it at every encounter, and thus to fight or flee as he chooses. Add to this that no animal appears to make war on man naturally, except in self-defense or from excessive hunger, nor to show any of those violent antipathies that seem to indicate that one species is intended by nature as the food of another.

This is doubtless why negroes and savages are so little afraid of the wild beasts they may meet in the woods. Among others, the Caraibs of Venezuela live in absolute security in this respect and without the smallest inconvenience. Francis Correal tells us that although they are almost naked, they expose themselves freely in the woods, armed only with bows and arrows. Yet no one has ever heard of one of them being devoured by wild beasts.

But man has other enemies that are more formidable, and against which he has no such means of defense. These are the natural infirmities of infancy, of old age, and of illness of every kind, melancholy proofs of our weakness. The first two are common to all animals, and the last belongs chiefly to man in a state of society. As to infancy, it can be observed that the mother always carries her child with her and so can nurse it with much greater ease than the females of many other animals. These are forced to keep going back and forth, with great fatigue, one way to find food and another to suckle or feed their young. It is true that if the woman happens to die, the infant is in great danger of dying with her. But this risk is common to many other species of animals, whose young take a long time to become able to provide for themselves. And if our infancy is longer than theirs, our lives are longer in proportion, so that in this respect all things are fairly equal. There are, though, other rules to be considered about the length of the first period of life and the number of young, and these do not affect the present subject. In old age, when men are less active and perspire little, the need for food shrinks along with the ability to provide it. The savage state also protects them from gout and rheumatism, and old age is, of all ills, the one that human aid can least relieve. So they cease to be without others noticing that they are no more, and almost without noticing it themselves.

As for sickness, I shall not repeat the vain and false declamations that most healthy people make against medicine. I shall ask instead whether any solid observation justifies concluding that men live shorter lives, on average, where medicine is most neglected than where it is most cultivated. How could that be, when we bring on ourselves more diseases than medicine can cure? Think of the great inequality in manner of living: some are extremely idle and others work to excess. Our sensual appetites are easily excited and gratified. The wealthy eat foods too exquisite, which overheat them and give them indigestion, while the poor eat unwholesome food, often too little of it even so, and are led, whenever they can, to gorge themselves and overload their stomachs. Think of late nights, of excesses of every kind, of immoderate transports of every passion, of fatigue, of mental exhaustion, and of the innumerable pains and anxieties that belong to every condition of life and torment the mind of man without rest. These are all too fatal proofs that most of our ills are of our own making, and that we could have avoided nearly all of them by keeping to the simple, uniform and solitary manner of life that nature prescribed. If she destined man to be healthy, I venture to declare that a state of reflection is a state contrary to nature, and that a thinking man is a depraved animal. Consider the good constitution of the savages, at least of those whom we have not ruined with our spirituous liquors, and consider that hardly any disorders trouble them except wounds and old age. We are then tempted to believe that, in following the history of civil society, we shall be telling the history of human sickness as well. Plato held this opinion at least. He inferred it from certain remedies that Podalirius and Machaon prescribed or approved at the siege of Troy: several sicknesses that those remedies caused in his own day, he said, were then unknown to mankind. And Celsus tells us that diet, so necessary now, was first invented by Hippocrates.

Man in the state of nature is subject to so few causes of sickness, and therefore can have no need of remedies, still less of physicians. In this respect the human race is no worse off than other animals, and it is easy to learn from hunters whether they meet many infirm animals in the course of the chase. It is certain that they often meet animals that bear the marks of having been badly wounded, and many that have had bones or even limbs broken, yet have been healed without any surgical help but that of time, or any other regimen than that of their ordinary life. Their cures seem to have been no less perfect for their not having been tortured by incisions, poisoned with drugs, or wasted by fasting. In short, medicine properly administered may be useful among us. Yet it is certain that if the savage, when he is sick and left to himself, has nothing to hope for except from nature, he has, on the other hand, nothing to fear except from his disease. This often makes his situation preferable to our own.

We should therefore beware of confusing the savage man with the men we see daily before our eyes. Nature treats all the animals left to her care with a partiality that seems to show how jealous she is of that right. The horse, the cat, the bull and even the ass are generally of greater stature, and always more robust, and have more vigor, strength and courage, when they run wild in the forests than when they are bred in the stall. By becoming domesticated, they lose half these advantages. It seems that all our care to feed and treat them well serves only to deprave them. It is the same with man. As he becomes sociable and a slave, he grows weak, timid and servile, and his effeminate way of life utterly enervates his strength and courage. It may be added that the difference between savage and civilized man is still greater than that between wild and tame beasts. Nature treated men and brutes alike, but men give themselves still more conveniences than they give their beasts, and these are so many additional causes of their deeper degeneracy.

It is therefore not so great a misfortune to these primitive men, nor so great an obstacle to their preservation, that they go naked, have no dwellings and lack all the superfluities that we think so necessary. If their skins are not covered with hair, they have no need of such covering in warm climates. In cold countries, they soon learn to take the skins of the beasts they have overcome. If they have only two legs to run with, they have two arms to defend themselves with and to provide for their wants. Their children are slow and have difficulty learning to walk, but their mothers can carry them with ease. Other animals lack this advantage, since a mother who is pursued is forced either to abandon her young or to match her pace to theirs. Unless we suppose, in short, a singular and fortuitous concurrence of circumstances, which I shall speak of later and which would be unlikely to exist, it is plain in every state of the case that the man who first made himself clothes or a dwelling was furnishing himself with things not at all necessary. For he had done without them until then, and there is no reason why he should not have been able to endure in manhood the same kind of life he had led in infancy.

The savage lives alone, in idleness, with danger always at his side, so he cannot help being fond of sleep. His sleep must also be light, like that of the animals, which think little and may be said to slumber for as long as they are not thinking. Self-preservation is his chief and almost sole concern. So the faculties he exercises most must be those that serve attack or defense, either to overcome his prey or to keep himself from becoming the prey of other animals. The organs that are perfected only by softness and sensuality, on the other hand, will stay gross and imperfect, and incompatible with any sort of delicacy. His senses will therefore be divided in this way: touch and taste extremely coarse, sight, hearing and smell exceedingly fine and subtle. This is the animal condition in general, and the narratives of travelers say it is also the condition of most savage nations. It is no wonder, then, that the Hottentots of the Cape of Good Hope can spot ships at sea with the naked eye from as far off as the Dutch can with their telescopes. Nor is it a wonder that the savages of America track the Spaniards by smell as well as the best dogs could, that these barbarous peoples feel no pain from going naked, that they season their food with great quantities of piemento, or that they drink the strongest European liquors like water.
So far I have considered only the physical man. Let us now look at him on his metaphysical and moral side.

In any animal I see only an ingenious machine. Nature has given it senses to wind itself up, and to protect itself, up to a point, from whatever might disorder or destroy it. I perceive exactly the same in the human machine, with one difference. In the operations of the brute, nature is the only agent. Man has a share in his own operations, as a free agent. The brute chooses and refuses by instinct, man by an act of free-will. So the brute cannot depart from the rule prescribed to it, even when departing would benefit it, while man often departs from such rules to his own harm. A pigeon would thus starve beside a dish of the choicest meats, and a cat on a heap of fruit or grain, though it is certain that either could find nourishment in the foods it scornfully rejects, if it thought of trying them. In the same way dissolute men run into excesses that bring on fevers and death, because the mind depraves the senses and the will goes on speaking when nature is silent.

Every animal has ideas, since it has senses, and it even combines those ideas to some degree. Man differs from the brute in this only by degree. Some philosophers have even maintained that there is a greater difference between one man and another than between some men and some beasts. So what sets man apart from the brute in kind is not so much understanding as the human quality of free-agency. Nature commands every animal, and the brute obeys. Man feels the same impulse, but knows he is at liberty to yield or to resist. It is above all in his consciousness of this liberty that the spirituality of his soul shows itself. Physics can explain, in some measure, how the senses work and how ideas form. But in the power of willing, or rather of choosing, and in the feeling of that power, we find only acts that are purely spiritual and that the laws of mechanism cannot explain at all.

Still, the difficulties that surround all these questions might leave room to dispute whether men and brutes differ in this way. There is another very specific quality that distinguishes them, and about it there can be no dispute. It is the faculty of self-improvement. Helped by circumstances, it gradually develops all our other faculties, and it belongs to the species as it does to the individual. A brute is, after a few months, all that he will ever be in his whole life, and his species after a thousand years is exactly what it was in the first year of that thousand. Why is man alone liable to become a dotard? Is it not because he returns, in this, to his primitive state? The brute has acquired nothing and so has nothing to lose, and it keeps the force of instinct. Man loses, through age or accident, all that his perfectibility had enabled him to gain, and so sinks lower than the brutes themselves. It would be melancholy to be forced to admit that this distinctive and almost unlimited faculty is the source of all human misfortunes. It would be melancholy to admit that it draws man, in time, out of his original state, in which he would have passed his days insensibly in peace and innocence. It would be melancholy to admit that this faculty, producing in successive ages his discoveries and his errors, his vices and his virtues, makes him at length a tyrant over himself and over nature.[1] It would be shocking to have to regard as a benefactor the man who first suggested to the Oroonoko Indians the use of the boards they apply to the temples of their children, which secure to them some part at least of their weakness and original happiness.

Nature leaves savage man solely to the direction of instinct, or rather she makes up for what instinct may lack with faculties that can at first take its place and afterwards raise him far above it. He must therefore begin with purely animal functions. Seeing and feeling must be his first condition, and he would share it with all other animals. To will and not to will, to desire and to fear, must be the first and almost the only operations of his soul, until new circumstances bring about new developments of his faculties.

Whatever moralists may hold, the human understanding owes a great deal to the passions, which, as everyone agrees, owe a great deal to the understanding in turn. The activity of the passions improves our reason. We want knowledge only because we wish to enjoy, and it is impossible to conceive why a person with no fears and no desires should trouble himself to reason. The passions, again, arise from our wants, and their progress depends on the progress of our knowledge. We can desire or fear a thing only through the idea we have of it, or through the simple impulse of nature. Now savage man has no intelligence of any kind, so he can have no passions except those of the second sort: his desires never go beyond his physical wants. The only goods he recognizes in the universe are food, a female, and sleep. The only evils he fears are pain and hunger. I say pain, and not death, because no animal can know what it is to die. Knowing death and its terrors is one of the first things man acquires when he departs from an animal state.

If it were necessary, it would be easy to support this opinion with facts. I could show that, among all the nations of the world, the understanding has advanced exactly in proportion to the wants that peoples received from nature or were subjected to by circumstances, and so in proportion to the passions that drove them to meet those needs. I might point to the arts, which arose in Egypt and spread with the flooding of the Nile. I might follow them into Greece, where they took root again, grew and towered to the skies among the rocks and sands of Attica, though they could not sprout on the fertile banks of the Eurotas. I might observe that the people of the North are in general more industrious than those of the South, because they cannot do as well without being so. It is as though nature wished to even things out by giving their understandings the fertility she had denied to their soil.

But who does not see, without turning to the uncertain testimony of history, that everything seems to take away from savage man both the temptation and the means to change his condition? His imagination paints no pictures, and his heart asks nothing of him. His few wants are so easily supplied, and he is so far from having the knowledge needed to want more, that he can have neither foresight nor curiosity. As nature grows familiar to him she grows indifferent to him. He always sees the same order in it, the same succession. He has not the understanding to wonder at the greatest miracles. Nor is it in his mind that we can expect to find the philosophy that man needs in order to notice, for once, what he sees every day. Nothing disturbs his soul, which is wholly absorbed in the feeling of its present existence, with no idea of the future, however near. His projects, as limited as his views, hardly reach to the end of the day. Such is the foresight of the native Caribean even now. He will improvidently sell you his cotton-bed in the morning, and come crying in the evening to buy it back, because he did not foresee that he would need it again the next night.

The more we reflect on this subject, the wider the distance appears between pure sensation and the simplest knowledge. Indeed, it is impossible to conceive how a man, by his own powers alone, with no help from communication and no spur from necessity, could have crossed so great a gap. How many ages may have passed before mankind could see any other fire than that of the heavens! What a multiplicity of chances must have occurred to teach them the commonest uses of that element! How often must they have let it go out before they learned to make it again? And how often may such a secret have died with the man who discovered it? What shall we say of agriculture? It is an art that demands so much labor and foresight, and relies so much on other arts, that it is plain it could only be practiced in a society that had at least begun. And its purpose is not so much to draw subsistence from the earth—the earth would produce that of itself—as to force it to produce what is most to our taste. But let us suppose that men had multiplied so much that the natural produce of the earth no longer sufficed to support them. This supposition, by the way, would prove that such a life was very advantageous to the human race. Let us suppose that the tools of husbandry dropped from the sky into the hands of savages, with no forges or workshops. Let us suppose that they overcame their natural aversion to continual labor, that they learned to look ahead to their needs, that they divined how to till the earth, sow grain and plant trees, and that they discovered how to grind corn and set the grape to ferment—all of which the gods must have taught them, since it is not to be conceived how they could discover such things for themselves. Even so, which of them would be so absurd as to take the trouble of cultivating a field that the first comer, man or beast, might strip of its crop if he took a liking to it? And how could each of them decide to pass his life in wearisome labor when, the more necessary the reward of his labor was to him, the surer he would be of not getting it? In a word, how could such a situation induce men to cultivate the earth, until it was regularly parcelled out among them, that is to say, until the state of nature had been abolished?

Suppose we took savage man to be as trained in the art of thinking as philosophers make him. Suppose we, like them, took him for a very philosopher, capable of investigating the sublimest truths and of forming, by highly abstract chains of reasoning, maxims of reason and justice, deduced from the love of order in general or the known will of his Creator. In a word, suppose we took him to be as intelligent and enlightened as he must have been, and is in fact found to have been, dull and stupid. What advantage would accrue to the species from all such metaphysics, which could not be communicated from one man to another, but must end with the man who made them? What progress could mankind make while dispersed in the woods among other animals? And how far could men improve or mutually enlighten one another when they had no fixed habitation and no need of one another's assistance, and the same persons hardly met twice in their lives, and perhaps then without knowing one another or speaking together?

Let us consider how many ideas we owe to the use of speech, and how far grammar trains the understanding and eases its operations. Let us reflect on the inconceivable pains and the infinite stretch of time that the first invention of languages must have cost. Add these reflections to what has gone before, and then judge how many thousand ages must have passed while the human mind slowly developed the operations of which it is capable.

Here I shall take the liberty of pausing for a moment over the difficulties concerning the origin of languages. On this subject I might content myself with simply repeating the investigations of the Abbé Condillac, since they fully confirm my system and perhaps even first suggested it. But it is plain, from the way this philosopher resolves the difficulties he himself raises about the origin of arbitrary signs, that he assumes what I question: namely, that a kind of society must already have existed among the first inventors of language. So while I refer the reader to his observations on this point, I think it right to give my own, in order to present the same difficulties in a light suited to my subject. The first that presents itself is to conceive how language can have become necessary. Men had no communication with one another and no need of any, so we can conceive neither the necessity of this invention nor its possibility, unless it was somehow indispensable. I might affirm, with many others, that languages arose in the domestic intercourse between parents and their children. But this expedient would not remove the difficulty, and it would also commit the blunder of those who, in reasoning on the state of nature, always import into it ideas gathered in a state of society. They constantly picture families living together under one roof, and the members of each keeping among themselves a union as intimate and lasting as the one we see among us, where so many common interests bind them together. In that first state, however, men had neither houses, nor huts, nor property of any kind whatever. Everyone lived where he could, seldom for more than a single night. The sexes came together without design, as accident, opportunity or inclination brought them, and they had no great need of words to tell each other their intentions; they parted with the same indifference. At first the mother nursed her children for her own sake, and afterwards, when habit had made them dear to her, for theirs. But as soon as the children were strong enough to go in search of their own food, they left her of their own accord. They had hardly any way of not losing one another except by staying continually within sight, and so they soon became quite unable to recognize one another when they happened to meet again. It is further to be observed that the child had all his wants to explain, and so had more to say to his mother than she had to say to him. He must therefore have borne the brunt of the work of invention, and the language he used would be of his own making. The number of languages would then be equal to the number of individuals speaking them, and the variety would be increased by their wandering, roving life, which gave no time for any idiom to become fixed. For to say that the mother dictated to her child the words he was to use in asking her for one thing or another explains how languages already formed are taught; it by no means explains how languages were first formed.

We will suppose, however, that this first difficulty is removed. Let us for a moment place ourselves on this side of the vast space that must lie between a pure state of nature and the state in which languages had become necessary. Admitting their necessity, let us inquire how they could first be established. Here we meet a new and worse difficulty. If men need speech in order to learn to think, they must have needed the art of thinking far more in order to invent the art of speaking. And even if we could conceive how the articulate sounds of the voice came to be taken as the conventional interpreters of our ideas, we should still have to ask what could have interpreted this convention for those ideas which answer to no sensible objects and so could be indicated neither by gesture nor by voice. We can therefore hardly form any tolerable conjectures about the origin of this art of communicating our thoughts and establishing a correspondence between minds. It is an art so sublime that, far distant as it is from its origin, philosophers still see it at such an immeasurable distance from perfection that no one is rash enough to affirm it will ever reach it. They would say so even if the revolutions that time necessarily produces were suspended in its favor, even if prejudice were banished from our academies or condemned to silence, and even if those learned societies devoted themselves without interruption, for whole ages, to this thorny question.

Mankind's first language, the most universal and the most vivid, was the simple cry of nature. In a word, it was the only language man needed before he had any occasion to persuade assembled multitudes by eloquence. Yet instinct alone drew this cry out of him, in urgent moments, to beg for help in danger or relief in pain. In the ordinary course of life, where gentler feelings prevail, it was of little use. Then men's ideas began to expand and multiply, and they came into closer communication. They strove to invent more numerous signs and a richer language. They multiplied the inflections of the voice and added gestures, which by nature say more and rely less on a prior agreement about their meaning. So visible and movable objects were expressed by gestures, and audible ones by imitative sounds. But gestures can point out hardly anything except objects that are present or easily described, and visible actions. They are not useful everywhere, since darkness or a solid object in the way destroys their effect. And besides, they rather ask for our attention than secure it. At length men therefore thought of putting in their place the articulate sounds of the voice. These sounds have no particular resemblance to any particular ideas, yet they are better fitted to express all of them, as conventional signs. Only common consent could set up such an institution, and it must have been carried out in a way not very easy for men whose gross organs had no practice in anything of the kind. It is also harder still to conceive in itself. Such a common agreement must have had motives, and speech seems to have been highly necessary before the use of it could be established.

It is reasonable to suppose that the first words mankind used meant much more than the words of languages already formed. Men did not know how discourse divides into its constituent parts, and so at first they gave every single word the sense of a whole proposition. Then they began to tell subject from attribute, and noun from verb, which was itself no common effort of genius. Substantives were at first nothing but proper names, and the present infinitive was the only tense of verbs. As for adjectives, the very idea of them must have been developed with great difficulty. Every adjective is an abstract idea, and abstractions are painful and unnatural operations.

At first every object received its own name, with no regard to genus or species. These first originators of language were in no position to tell genera from species, and each individual stood alone in their minds, as individuals do in the picture of nature. One oak was called A, another B. The first idea we form of two things is that they are not the same, and it often takes a long time to see what they have in common. So the narrower their knowledge of things, the larger their dictionary must have been. Such a vocabulary was hard to use, and the difficulty could not easily be removed. To arrange beings under common and generic names, one has to know their distinguishing properties. That needed observation and definition, in other words a natural history and a metaphysics far more advanced than men of that time can have had.

Add that general ideas cannot enter the mind without the help of words, and the understanding grasps them only through propositions. This is one reason why animals cannot form such ideas, nor ever acquire the capacity for self-improvement that depends on them. A monkey goes from one nut to another. Are we to conceive that he has some general idea of that kind of fruit and compares its archetype with the two individual nuts? Assuredly not. The sight of one nut recalls to his memory the sensations the other gave him, and his eyes, modified in a certain way, tell his palate what modification it is about to receive. Every general idea is purely intellectual. Let the imagination meddle with it ever so little, and the idea at once becomes particular. Try to trace in your mind the image of a tree in general, and you will never succeed. Whatever you do, you will have to see it as large or small, bare or leafy, light or dark. If you could see in it only what all trees share, it would no longer look like a tree at all. Purely abstract beings are perceived in the same way, or can be conceived only through language. Only the definition of a triangle gives you a true idea of it. As soon as you picture a triangle in your mind, it is some particular triangle and no other, and you cannot help giving it visible lines and a colored area. So we must use propositions and language to form general ideas. For once the imagination stops working, the understanding goes forward only by means of words. If the first inventors of speech could name only the ideas they already had, it follows that the first substantives could be nothing more than proper names.

But our new grammarians began, by means I cannot conceive, to extend their ideas and to generalize their terms. The ignorance of the inventors must have confined this method within very narrow limits. They had at first gone too far in multiplying the names of individuals, through ignorance of their genus and species. Afterwards they made too few names, through not having considered beings in all their specific differences. To carry these distinctions far enough would indeed have required more knowledge and experience than they could have had, and more pains and inquiry than they would have been willing to spend. Even today we are continually discovering new species that have escaped observation until now. Let us reflect how many of them must have escaped men who judged things merely by their first appearance! It is needless to add that the first classes and the most general notions must necessarily have escaped their notice also. How, for instance, could they have understood or even thought of the words matter, spirit, substance, mode, figure, motion? Our own philosophers, who have used them for so long, have the greatest difficulty in understanding them themselves. And since the ideas attached to them are purely metaphysical, no models of them are to be found in nature.

But I stop here, and I ask my judges to put down their reading for a while. Let them consider that physical substantives are the easiest part of language to invent. Even after they were invented, there was still a long way to go before men's thoughts could find perfect expression and a fixed form, fit for public speaking and able to take effect on society. I beg them to consider how much time and how much knowledge it must have taken to find out numbers, abstract terms, aorists and all the tenses of verbs, particles, syntax, the way of connecting propositions, the forms of reasoning, and all the logic of speech. As for me, the difficulties pile up so fast that I am aghast. I am so convinced, too, that it is almost demonstrably impossible for languages to have originated by merely human means, that I leave to anyone willing to take it up the discussion of this difficult problem: which was more necessary, a society already in existence for the invention of language, or language already invented for the establishment of society. But whatever the origin of language and society may be, one thing at least can be inferred. Nature has taken little care to unite mankind through mutual wants or to make speech easy to use. From this we may infer that she has done little to make men sociable, and has put little of her own into all they have done to build such bonds of union.
