Indeed it is impossible to conceive why, in a state of nature, one man should need another's assistance any more than a monkey or a wolf needs the help of another of its kind. Or suppose he did need it: then I cannot conceive what motives could induce the other to assist him, or even then how they could agree about the conditions. I know people say over and over that man in such a state would have been the most miserable of creatures. Yet if it is true, as I think I have proved, that he must have lived many ages before he could have either the desire or the opportunity to leave that state, this would be an accusation against nature alone, not against the being she had so unhappily constituted. As I understand the word miserable, it has no meaning at all, or else it signifies only a painful privation of something, or a state of suffering in body or soul. I should be glad to be told what kind of misery a free being can possibly suffer, when his heart is at ease and his body in health. I would ask also which life is more likely to become unbearable to those who live it, the social or the natural. Around us we see hardly a creature in civil society who does not lament his existence. We even see many take away as much of it as they can from themselves, and laws human and divine together can hardly stop this disorder. I ask whether anyone has ever heard of a savage at liberty who took it into his head to complain of life or to make away with himself. Let us therefore judge, with less vanity, on which side the real misery lies. By contrast, nothing could be more unhappy than savage man dazzled by science, tormented by his passions, and reasoning about a state different from his own. It appears that Providence most wisely ordained that the faculties he potentially possessed should develop only as occasions arose to exercise them. They would then not be superfluous and perplexing to him by appearing before their time, nor slow and useless when the need for them came. In instinct alone he had everything he required to live in the state of nature; with a developed understanding he has barely enough to sustain life in society.

At first view it appears that men in a state of nature had no moral relations or determinate obligations to one another, and so could be neither good nor bad, neither virtuous nor vicious. That holds unless we take these terms in a physical sense, calling vices in an individual the qualities that may harm his preservation, and virtues the ones that contribute to it. In that case, the most virtuous man would be the one who put the least check on the pure impulses of nature. Yet without leaving the ordinary meaning of the words, it is proper to suspend any judgment we might form of such a state, and to guard against our prejudices. We must first weigh the matter in the scales of impartiality. We must see whether virtues or vices preponderate among civilized men, and whether their virtues do them more good than their vices do harm. We must discover whether the progress of the sciences sufficiently repays them for the mischief they do one another, in proportion as they learn more of the good they ought to do. Or we must see whether they would not be, on the whole, far happier with nothing to fear or hope from anyone, than they are now, when they depend on everyone and must take everything from those who undertake to give them nothing in return.

Above all, let us not conclude with Hobbes that man is naturally wicked because he has no idea of goodness. Let us not say that he is vicious because he does not know virtue, that he always refuses to do his fellow creatures services he thinks they have no right to demand, or that he foolishly imagines himself the sole proprietor of the whole universe by virtue of the right he truly claims to everything he needs. Hobbes saw clearly the defects of all the modern definitions of natural right. But the consequences he draws from his own definition show that he understands it in an equally false sense. Reasoning from the principles he lays down, he ought to have said this: the state of nature is the state in which care for our own preservation does the least harm to the preservation of others, and it was therefore the best suited to peace and the most fitting for mankind. He says exactly the opposite. The reason is that he wrongly counted among savage man's care for self-preservation the gratification of a multitude of passions, which are the work of society and have made laws necessary. A bad man, he says, is a robust child. But it remains to be proved whether man in a state of nature is this robust child. And if we grant that he is, what would Hobbes conclude? Why, truly, that if this man, robust and strong, depended on others as he does when feeble, there is no extravagance he would not commit. He would beat his mother when she was slow to give him her breast. He would strangle one of his younger brothers if he were troublesome, or bite another's arm if he put him to any inconvenience. But to say that man in the state of nature is both strong and dependent is to make two contrary suppositions. Man is weak when he is dependent, and he is his own master before he becomes strong. Hobbes did not reflect that one and the same cause keeps the savage from using his reason, as our jurists hold, and keeps him from abusing his faculties, as Hobbes himself allows. So it may justly be said that savages are not bad merely because they do not know what it is to be good. Neither the development of the understanding nor the restraint of law keeps them from doing ill. What does is the peacefulness of their passions and their ignorance of vice: tanto plus in illis proficit vitiorum ignoratio, quam in his cognitio virtutis.[2] Hobbes missed another principle. It was given to mankind to moderate, on certain occasions, the impetuosity of egoism, or, before egoism was born, the desire of self-preservation. It tempers the ardor with which man pursues his own welfare by an innate repugnance at seeing a fellow creature suffer.[3] I think I need not fear contradiction when I say that man possesses the one natural virtue that even the most violent detractor of human virtue could not deny him. I am speaking of compassion. It is a disposition suited to creatures as weak and as exposed to so many evils as we certainly are. It is the more universal and useful to mankind because it comes before any kind of reflection, and at the same time so natural that the very brutes sometimes give clear proofs of it. I need not mention the tenderness of mothers for their offspring and the perils they face to save them. It is well known that horses are reluctant to trample on living bodies. An animal never passes by the dead body of another of its species. Some even give their fellows a sort of burial, and the mournful lowing of cattle as they enter the slaughter-house shows what the horrible sight there does to them. We find it a pleasure that the author of the Fable of the Bees was obliged to admit that man is a compassionate and sensible being. In his example he lays aside his cold subtlety of style and gives us a pathetic picture of a man shut in a place of confinement and forced to watch a wild beast tear a child from its mother's arms. The beast grinds the tender limbs with its murderous teeth and tears the palpitating entrails with its claws. What horrid agitation the eye-witness of such a scene must feel, although he is not personally concerned! What anxiety he must suffer at being unable to help the fainting mother and the dying infant!

Such is the pure emotion of nature, before any kind of reflection! Such is the force of natural compassion, which the deepest depravity of morals has so far hardly been able to destroy! Every day at our theaters we see men moved to tears by the sufferings of a wretch who, in the tyrant's place, would probably add to the torments of his enemies. So it was with the bloodthirsty Sulla, who felt so keenly for ills he had not caused. So it was with that Alexander of Pheros, who dared not attend any tragedy, for fear of being seen weeping with Andromache and Priam, though he could hear without emotion the cries of all the citizens who were strangled daily at his command.
Mollissima corda Humano generi dare se natura fatetur, Qua lacrimas dedit. Juvenal, Satire xv, 151.[4]

Mandeville understood well that, for all their morality, men would never have been better than monsters if nature had not given them compassion to aid their reason. What he did not see is that all the social virtues, which he denied man possessed, flow from this one quality. For what are generosity, clemency and humanity if not compassion directed at the weak, at the guilty, or at mankind in general? Even benevolence and friendship, if we judge rightly, are only the effects of a compassion constantly fixed on one particular object. For is it any different to wish that a person may not suffer pain and uneasiness, and to wish him happy? Suppose it were even true that pity is no more than a feeling that puts us in the place of the sufferer, a feeling obscure yet lively in a savage, developed yet feeble in civilized man. This truth would only confirm my argument. Compassion must in fact be stronger, the more completely the animal that beholds any kind of distress identifies with the animal that suffers. Now it is plain that this identification must have been far more perfect in a state of nature than it is in a state of reason. Reason engenders self-respect, and reflection confirms it. Reason turns man's mind back upon itself and divides him from everything that could disturb or afflict him. Philosophy isolates him, and bids him say, at the sight of the misfortunes of others: "Perish if you will, I am secure." Only such general evils as threaten the whole community can disturb the tranquil sleep of the philosopher or drag him from his bed. Someone may be murdered under his window with impunity. He has only to put his hands over his ears and argue a little with himself, and he stops nature, which is shocked within him, from identifying itself with the unfortunate victim. Uncivilized man lacks this admirable talent. For want of reason and wisdom, he is always foolishly ready to obey the first promptings of humanity. In riots and street-brawls it is the populace that crowds together, while the wise man prudently makes off. It is the mob and the market-women who separate the combatants and stop gentlefolk from cutting one another's throats.

It is then certain that compassion is a natural feeling. By moderating the violence of love of self in each individual, it contributes to the preservation of the whole species. Compassion hurries us, without reflection, to the relief of those in distress. In a state of nature it takes the place of laws, morals and virtues, with the advantage that no one is tempted to disobey its gentle voice. It will always keep a sturdy savage from robbing a weak child or a feeble old man of the food they have gathered with pain and difficulty, if he sees any chance of providing for himself elsewhere. It does not teach that sublime maxim of rational justice, Do to others as you would have them do unto you. It inspires all men instead with that other maxim of natural goodness, much less perfect indeed, but perhaps more useful: Do good to yourself with as little evil as possible to others. In a word, the cause of the repugnance every man feels at doing evil, even apart from the maxims of education, is to be found in this natural feeling rather than in any subtle arguments. Socrates and other minds of the same craft might be able to acquire virtue by reason. But the human race would long since have ceased to exist if its preservation had depended only on the reasonings of the individuals composing it.

Their passions were so little active and so well curbed that men were rather wild than wicked. They cared more about guarding themselves against the mischief that might be done them than about doing mischief to others, so they were by no means exposed to very perilous dissensions. They had no kind of intercourse with one another, and were consequently strangers to vanity, deference, esteem and contempt. They had not the least idea of meum and tuum, and no true conception of justice. Any violence done to them they took as an injury easily repaired, not as a crime to be punished. They never thought of taking revenge, unless perhaps mechanically and on the spot, as a dog will sometimes bite the stone thrown at him. Their quarrels would therefore seldom have had very bloody consequences, since the only thing at stake would be subsistence. But I am aware of one greater danger, which remains to be noticed.

One of the passions that stir the heart of man makes the sexes necessary to each other. It is extremely ardent and impetuous. It is a terrible passion that braves danger and surmounts all obstacles, and in its transports it seems fit to bring destruction on the very human race it is destined to preserve. What is to become of men abandoned to this brutal and boundless rage, without modesty, without shame, and daily keeping up their love affairs at the price of their blood?

In the first place, it must be allowed that the more violent the passions are, the more laws are needed to keep them in restraint. But leave aside how inadequate laws are to this purpose, as the crimes and disorders these passions cause among us every day make evident. We should do well to ask whether these evils did not spring up together with the laws. For in that case, even if the laws could repress such evils, the least we could expect of them is that they check a mischief that would not have arisen without them.

Let us begin by distinguishing the physical from the moral ingredients in the feeling of love. The physical part is that general desire which drives the sexes toward union with each other. The moral part is what fixes this desire on one particular object to the exclusion of others, or at least gives it greater force toward the object preferred. It is easy to see that the moral part of love is an artificial feeling. It is born of social usage, and women have fostered it with great care and cleverness in order to establish their empire and put in power the sex that ought to obey. This feeling rests on certain ideas of beauty and merit which a savage is in no position to acquire, and on comparisons which he is incapable of making. For him it must therefore be almost non-existent. His mind cannot form abstract ideas of proportion and regularity, and so his heart is not open to the feelings of love and admiration that these ideas produce, even without our noticing. He follows only the character nature has implanted in him, not tastes he could never have acquired, and so every woman equally serves his purpose.

Men in a state of nature are confined to what is physical in love. They are fortunate enough to be ignorant of those excellences which sharpen the appetite while they make it harder to satisfy. They must therefore be subject to fewer and less violent fits of passion, and so they fall into fewer and less violent quarrels. The imagination, which causes such ravages among us, never speaks to the heart of savages. They quietly await the impulses of nature and yield to them involuntarily, with more pleasure than ardor; and once their wants are satisfied, the desire is gone. It is therefore beyond dispute that love, like all the other passions, must have acquired in society that glowing impetuosity which so often makes it fatal to mankind. It is all the more absurd to portray savages as continually cutting one another's throats to indulge their brutality, because this opinion is directly contrary to experience. The Caribeans, who have so far deviated least of all from the state of nature, are in fact the most peaceable of people in their love affairs and the least subject to jealousy, though they live in a hot climate which seems always to inflame the passions.

Someone may draw inferences from certain species of animals. Their males fill our poultry-yards with blood and slaughter, or in spring make the forests ring with their quarrels over the females. We must first set aside every species in which nature has plainly arranged the comparative power of the sexes differently from the way it stands among us; thus the habits of fighting cocks allow no conclusion about men. In the species where the proportion is better kept, these battles can only come from the scarcity of females compared with males. Or, what comes to the same thing, they come from the intervals when the female constantly refuses the male: if each female accepts the male for only two months of the year, it is as if the females were five-sixths fewer. Now neither case fits the human species. Among men the females usually outnumber the males, and no one has ever observed, even among savages, that the females have, like those of other animals, fixed seasons of passion and indifference. Moreover, in several of these species all the individuals take fire together, and a fearful moment arrives of universal passion, tumult and disorder among them. Nothing of the kind is ever seen in the human species, whose love is not seasonal. We must not then conclude from the combats of such animals over the females that the same would hold for mankind in a state of nature. Even if we did conclude it, we see that such contests do not wipe out other kinds of animals, and we have no reason to think they would be deadlier among ours. It is indeed clear that they would do still less harm than they do in a state of society. That is above all true in those countries where morals are still held in some repute, and where the jealousy of lovers and the vengeance of husbands cause duels, murders and even worse crimes every day; where the obligation of eternal fidelity only breeds adultery, and the very laws of honor and continence necessarily increase debauchery and multiply abortions.

Let us conclude, then, that man in a state of nature has no industry, no speech and no home, but wanders up and down the forests. He is as much a stranger to war as to every tie. He has no need of his fellow creatures and no desire to harm them, and perhaps does not even tell one from another. Let us conclude also that, being self-sufficient and subject to so few passions, he could have only such feelings and knowledge as befitted his situation. He felt only his actual necessities. He paid no attention to anything he did not think himself immediately concerned to notice, and his understanding advanced no further than his vanity. If he happened to make a discovery, he was the less able to pass it on, because he did not even know his own children. Every art would necessarily die with its inventor, where men had no kind of education and generation followed generation without the least advance. All started from the same point, and so centuries must have gone by in the barbarism of the first ages; the race was already old, and man remained a child.

I have lingered at such length over this supposed primitive state because I had so many ancient errors and deep-rooted prejudices to uproot. I thought it my duty to dig down to their very root. By a true picture of the state of nature I meant to show how far even the natural inequalities of mankind fall short of the reality and influence that modern writers suppose.

It is in fact easy to see that many differences between men are only the effect of habit and of the different ways of life men take up in society. A robust or delicate constitution, and the strength or weakness that goes with it, come more often from a hardy or soft upbringing than from the body's original endowment. The same is true of the powers of the mind. Education creates a difference between the cultured and the uncultured, and it even widens the differences among the cultured, in proportion to how far each has been cultivated. It is like a giant and a dwarf on the same road: the distance between them grows with every step they take. Now set the prodigious diversity of education and manner of life among the various orders of men in the state of society beside the uniformity and simplicity of animal and savage life, where all eat the same food, live in exactly the same manner and do exactly the same things. Then it is easy to conceive how much less men must differ from one another in a state of nature than in a state of society, and how greatly the inequalities of social institutions must increase the natural inequality of mankind.

But suppose nature really did show, in handing out her gifts, that partiality which is charged against her. What advantage could her greatest favorites gain from it, at the expense of others, in a state that scarcely allows any relation between them? Where there is no love, what good is beauty? What use is wit to people who do not converse, or cunning to people who have no business with one another? I hear it said again and again that in such a state the strong would oppress the weak. But what do we mean here by oppression? Some, it is said, would dominate others by force, and the others would groan under servile submission to their caprices. That is indeed exactly what I see happening among us; but I do not see how it can be inferred of men in a state of nature, who could hardly be brought to understand what we mean by dominion and servitude. One man, it is true, might seize the fruits another had gathered, the game he had killed or the cave he had chosen for shelter. But how would he ever manage to exact obedience, and what ties of dependence could exist among men who own nothing? If, for instance, I am driven from one tree, I can go to the next; if I am disturbed in one place, what stops me from going to another? Again, suppose I happen to meet a man so much stronger than I am, and at the same time so depraved, so indolent and so barbarous, that he forces me to feed him while he himself sits idle. He must never take his eyes off me for a single moment, and he must tie me up before he goes to sleep, or I shall certainly either knock him on the head or escape. That is to say, in such a case he must willingly take on far more trouble than he seeks to avoid, or than he can give me. After all this, let him relax his guard ever so little; let him but turn his head at some sudden noise, and I shall be twenty paces off in an instant, lost in the forest. My fetters burst apart, and he would never see me again.

There is no need for me to dwell uselessly on these details; everyone must see that the bonds of servitude arise only from men's mutual dependence and the reciprocal needs that unite them. It is therefore impossible to enslave a man unless he has first been put in a situation where he cannot do without the help of others. Such a situation does not exist in a state of nature. There everyone is his own master, and the law of the strongest has no effect.

I have proved that in a state of nature the inequality of mankind is hardly felt and its influence is next to nothing. I must now show how it arose and trace its progress through the successive developments of the human mind. I have shown that human perfectibility, the social virtues and the other faculties that natural man possessed only potentially could never develop of themselves. For that they needed the chance coming-together of many outside causes that might never occur, and without them he would have stayed forever in his primitive condition. I must now collect and consider the different accidents that may have improved the human understanding while depraving the species, and made man wicked while making him sociable. By these I shall bring him and the world from that distant period to the point where we now see them.

I confess that the events I am about to describe might have happened in various ways, so that conjectures alone guide my choice. Yet conjectures become reasons when they are the most probable that can be drawn from the nature of things, and the only means we have of discovering the truth. Nor will the consequences I mean to deduce be merely conjectural. On the principles just laid down, no other theory could be formed that would not yield the same results, and from which I could not draw the same conclusions.

This will be a sufficient apology for my not dwelling on several matters: how the passage of time makes up for the slight probability of the events; how surprisingly powerful trivial causes are when they act constantly; how certain hypotheses cannot be destroyed, though we cannot give them the certainty of known matters of fact; how it is the business of history, when two facts are given as real and must be joined by a series of intermediate facts that are unknown or supposed to be so, to supply the facts that join them, and the business of philosophy, when history is silent, to determine similar facts for the same purpose; and lastly, how similarity influences events, reducing the facts to a much smaller number of different classes than is commonly imagined. It is enough for me to offer these hints to the consideration of my judges, and to have arranged things so that the general reader need not consider them at all.

chapters.title: Part 2
paragraphs: The real founder of civil society was the first man who enclosed a piece of ground, thought of saying This is mine, and found people simple enough to believe him. How many crimes, wars and murders, how many horrors and misfortunes, might anyone have spared mankind by pulling up the stakes or filling in the ditch and crying out to his fellows, "Beware of listening to this impostor; you are undone if you once forget that the fruits of the earth belong to us all, and the earth itself to nobody." But it is very probable that things had by then already reached a point where they could no longer go on as they were. For the idea of property depends on many earlier ideas, which could be acquired only one after another, and cannot have formed in the human mind all at once.

Mankind must have made very considerable progress before reaching this last point of the state of nature. They must have gained a good deal of knowledge and industry, and handed it down and added to it from age to age. Let us then go further back, and try to bring that slow succession of events and discoveries under a single view, in the most natural order.

The first feeling of man was that of his own existence, and his first care was self-preservation. The earth's produce gave him everything he needed, and instinct told him how to use it. Hunger and other appetites made him experience different ways of existing at different times. Among them was one that urged him to propagate his species—a blind propensity, which had nothing to do with the heart and produced a purely animal act. Once the want was satisfied, the two sexes knew each other no more. Even the child meant nothing to its mother as soon as it could do without her.

Such was the condition of infant man. His was the life of an animal, limited at first to mere sensations, scarcely profiting from the gifts nature offered him, and far from thinking of wresting anything from her. But difficulties soon arose, and he had to learn to overcome them. The trees were tall and kept him from gathering their fruits; other animals wanted the same fruits and competed for them; and those who needed them for their own preservation were fierce. All this obliged him to train his body. He had to be active, swift of foot and vigorous in fight. Natural weapons, stones and sticks, were easy to find. He learned to overcome the obstacles of nature, to fight other animals when he had to, to dispute the means of subsistence even with other men, or to make up for what he was forced to yield to a stronger.

As the human race grew more numerous, men had more to care for. Soils, climates and seasons differ, and this must have brought differences into their way of living. Barren years, long and bitter winters, and summers that scorched and parched the fruits of the earth must have demanded new industry. Along the sea-shore and the banks of rivers they invented the hook and line, and became fishermen and eaters of fish. In the forests they made bows and arrows, and became huntsmen and warriors. In cold countries they wore the skins of the beasts they had killed. Lightning, a volcano or some lucky chance showed them fire, a new resource against the rigors of winter. Next they learned to keep this element alive, then to produce it again, and finally to cook with it the flesh of animals that they had eaten raw before.

Man met various beings again and again, and found them bearing on himself and on one another. This would naturally give rise in the human mind to the perception of certain relations between them. We express these relations by the terms great, small, strong, weak, swift, slow, fearful, bold, and the like. Compared almost without his noticing, whenever the need arose, they must at length have produced in him a kind of reflection, or rather a mechanical prudence, which showed him the precautions most necessary for his security.

The new intelligence that came of this development increased his superiority over other animals, by making him aware of it. He would now try to trap them, play a thousand tricks on them, and in time become the master of some and the scourge of others, although many of them might surpass him in swiftness or strength. Thus, the first time he looked into himself, he felt the first emotion of pride. At a time when he scarcely knew how to tell the different orders of beings apart, he looked on his own species as of the highest order, and so prepared the way for claiming pre-eminence as an individual.

It is true that other men were not then to him what they are now to us, and he had no more dealings with them than with other animals. Yet he did not neglect them in his observations. In time he would discover resemblances between them, and between himself and his female, and these led him to judge of others that were not yet perceptible. He found that they all behaved as he would himself have done in like circumstances, and so he naturally inferred that their way of thinking and acting was altogether like his own. This important truth, once deeply impressed on his mind, must have led him, by an intuitive feeling more certain and much more rapid than any reasoning, to follow the rules of conduct which it was best for him to observe toward them, for his own security and advantage.

From experience he learned that the love of well-being is the sole motive of human actions. This let him pick out the few cases where mutual interest justified relying on the help of his fellows, and the still fewer cases where a conflict of interests gave cause to distrust them. In the first kind of case, he joined them in a herd, or at most in some loose association that placed no restraint on its members and lasted only as long as the passing occasion that formed it. In the second kind, each man sought his own private advantage. If he thought himself strong enough, he used open force; if he felt himself the weaker, he used address and cunning.

In this way men may have slowly picked up some crude ideas of mutual undertakings and of the advantages of keeping them. But they grasped these only so far as their present and apparent interest was concerned, for they were perfect strangers to foresight. They did not trouble themselves about the distant future; they hardly thought of the morrow. Suppose a deer was to be taken. Everyone saw that to succeed he must keep faithfully to his post. But if a hare happened to pass within reach of any one of them, it is not to be doubted that he went after it without scruple. Once he had seized his prey, he cared very little that his companions had missed theirs because of it.

It is easy to see that such dealings would not need a language much more refined than that of rooks or monkeys, which flock together for much the same purpose. For a long time the universal language must have consisted of inarticulate cries, plenty of gestures and some imitative sounds. Each country then added some conventional articulate sounds (the first institution of which, as I have already intimated, is not easy to explain), and this produced particular languages. They were rude and imperfect, however, and very like those still found among some savage nations.

Time rushes me on, and so does the abundance of things I have to say, and so does the almost imperceptible progress of things in their beginnings. I therefore pass over a multitude of ages in an instant. The slower the events followed one another, the more quickly they can be described.

These first advances let men make further ones more quickly. The more enlightened they became, the more industrious they grew. They no longer fell asleep under the first tree, or in the first cave that sheltered them. They invented several kinds of implements out of hard and sharp stones, and used them to dig the earth and cut wood. Then they built huts of branches, and afterwards learned to plaster these with mud and clay. This was the epoch of a first revolution. It established and distinguished families, and brought in a kind of property, itself the source of a thousand quarrels and conflicts. Now the strongest were probably the first to build huts they felt able to defend. We may conclude that the weak found it much easier and safer to imitate them than to try to dislodge them. And once a man had a hut, he could have no inducement to appropriate his neighbor's. This was not so much because the hut was not his, as because it would be of no use to him, and he could not make himself master of it without a desperate battle with the family living in it.

The first expansions of the human heart came from a new situation, which brought husbands and wives, fathers and children together under one roof. Living together by habit soon gave rise to the finest feelings humanity knows, conjugal love and paternal affection. Every family became a little society, and the more united because liberty and reciprocal attachment were the only bonds holding it together. The sexes had lived in the same way until then; now they began to adopt different ways of living. The women grew more sedentary and accustomed themselves to looking after the hut and the children, while the men went abroad to find their common subsistence. Both sexes, living more softly, began to lose something of their strength and ferocity. Individuals may to some extent have become less able to face wild beasts separately, but on the other hand they found it easier to gather and resist in common.

Man's life in this new condition was simple and solitary, his wants were few, and the implements he had invented to meet them left him a great deal of leisure. He spent it furnishing himself with many conveniences his fathers had not known. This was the first yoke he unwittingly laid on himself, and the first source of the evils he prepared for his descendants. For these conveniences continued to enervate body and mind. With use they also lost almost all their power to please, and even degenerated into real needs. Lacking them became far more disagreeable than having them had been pleasant. Men would have been unhappy to lose them, although having them did not make them happy.

Here we can see a little better how the use of speech became established and slowly improved in each family. We may also form a conjecture how various causes may have spread and quickened the progress of language, by making it more and more necessary. Floods or earthquakes cut off inhabited districts with precipices or waters. Revolutions of the globe tore portions off the continent and made them islands. It is easy to see that men gathered together in this way and compelled to live close to one another would develop a common idiom much more readily than men still wandering the forests of the continent. So it is very possible that the islanders, after their first trials at navigation, carried the use of speech over to the continent. At the least it is very probable that communities and languages were first established in islands, and even reached perfection there before the mainland knew them.

Everything now begins to change its aspect. Men who had roamed the woods settle into a more fixed way of life, come gradually together and form separate bodies. At length every country has a distinct nation, held together in character and manners not by regulations or laws but by a uniform life and food and the common influence of climate. Living permanently near one another could not fail, in time, to produce some connection between different families. Young people of opposite sexes lived in neighboring huts. The passing commerce nature requires soon led, through their mutual intercourse, to another kind just as agreeable and more lasting. Men began to notice the differences between objects and to make comparisons. Without noticing, they acquired ideas of beauty and merit, and these soon gave rise to feelings of preference. Seeing each other often, they could not do without seeing each other constantly. A tender and pleasant feeling crept into their souls, and the least opposition turned it to impetuous fury. Jealousy arose with love; discord triumphed, and human blood was sacrificed to the gentlest of all passions.

Ideas and feelings followed one another, and heart and head came into play. Men went on laying aside their original wildness, and their private connections grew more intimate every day as their limits widened. They got used to gathering before their huts round a large tree. Singing and dancing, the true offspring of love and leisure, became the amusement, or rather the occupation, of the men and women who gathered there with nothing else to do. Each began to consider the rest and to wish to be considered in turn. Thus public esteem came to carry a value. The best singer or dancer, the handsomest, the strongest, the most dexterous or the most eloquent, came to be the most considered. This was the first step toward inequality, and at the same time toward vice. These first distinctions gave rise to vanity and contempt on the one side, and to shame and envy on the other. The fermentation caused by these new leavens ended by producing combinations fatal to innocence and happiness.

As soon as men began to value one another, and the idea of consideration took hold of the mind, everyone put in his claim to it, and no one could refuse it to anyone with impunity. This was the origin of the first obligations of civility, even among savages. It also turned every intended injury into an affront. Besides the hurt it might cause, the injured party was sure to see in it contempt for his person, and this was often more unbearable than the hurt itself.

Thus every man punished the contempt shown him by others in proportion to his opinion of himself, and so revenge became terrible, and men bloody and cruel. This is precisely the state reached by most of the savage nations known to us. Many writers have hastily concluded that man is naturally cruel and needs civil institutions to make him more mild. They have done so for want of making a proper distinction in our ideas, and of seeing how very far these nations already are from the state of nature. Yet nothing is more gentle than man in his primitive state, where nature places him at an equal distance from the stupidity of brutes and the fatal ingenuity of civilized man. Instinct and reason equally confine him to the sole care of guarding himself against the mischiefs that threaten him. Natural compassion restrains him from doing any injury to others, and does not lead him to do such a thing even in return for injuries received. For, according to the axiom of the wise Locke, There can be no injury, where there is no property.

But it must be remarked that the society so formed, and the relations so established among men, called for qualities different from those they had by their primitive constitution. Morality began to appear in human actions. Before law was instituted, each man was the only judge and avenger of the injuries done to him. The goodness suited to the pure state of nature was therefore no longer fitting in the new-born state of society. As opportunities of offending became more frequent, punishments had to be made more severe, and the dread of vengeance had to take the place of the rigor of the law. So men had become less patient, and their natural compassion had already lost something. Still, this period, when the human faculties expanded and kept a just mean between the indolence of the primitive state and the petulant activity of our egoism, must have been the happiest and most stable of epochs. The more we reflect on it, the more we shall find that this state was the least subject to revolutions, and altogether the best that man could experience. He can have left it only through some fatal accident, which, for the public good, should never have happened. Savages, most of whom have been found in this state, seem by their example to prove that men were meant to remain in it, that it is the real youth of the world, and that every later advance has seemed a step toward the perfection of the individual but has in reality been a step toward the decrepitude of the species.

Men were content with their rustic huts. They were satisfied with clothes of animal skins sewn together with thorns and fish-bones. They adorned themselves only with feathers and shells, kept painting their bodies different colors, improved and beautified their bows and arrows, and used sharp-edged stones to make fishing boats or clumsy musical instruments. In a word, they undertook only what one person could accomplish alone, and kept to arts that did not need the joint labor of several hands. As long as this lasted, they lived free, healthy, honest and happy lives, as far as their nature allowed, and kept enjoying the pleasures of mutual and independent intercourse. But once one man needed the help of another, and once it appeared advantageous for anyone to have enough provisions for two, equality disappeared, property was introduced, and work became indispensable. Vast forests became smiling fields, which man had to water with the sweat of his brow, and slavery and misery were soon seen to germinate and grow up with the crops.

Two arts produced this great revolution: metallurgy and agriculture. The poets say it was gold and silver; the philosophers say it was iron and corn that first civilized men and ruined humanity. The savages of America knew neither, and for that reason they are still savage. The other nations too seem to have stayed in a state of barbarism as long as they practiced only one of these arts. Perhaps one of the best reasons why Europe has been more constantly and highly civilized than the rest of the world, if not for longer, is that it is at once the most abundant in iron and the most fertile in corn.

How men first came to know and use iron is hard to conjecture. We cannot suppose they would of themselves think of digging ore out of a mine and preparing it for smelting before they knew what would come of it. Nor have we much reason to suppose some accidental fire made the discovery, since mines form only in barren places, bare of trees and plants. It looks as if nature had taken pains to keep the fatal secret from us. Only the extraordinary accident of a volcano remains. By throwing out metallic substances already in fusion, it suggested to the onlookers the idea of imitating what nature did. We must also conceive them as having uncommon courage and foresight, to undertake so laborious a work with so distant a prospect of advantage. Yet such qualities are found together only in minds more advanced than we can suppose those of the first discoverers to have been.

The principles of agriculture were known long before they were put in practice. Indeed it is hardly possible that men who constantly drew their subsistence from plants and trees should not readily learn how nature propagates vegetables. In all probability, however, it was very long before their industry took that turn. Perhaps trees, which together with hunting and fishing gave them food, needed no attention from them. Or they did not know the use of corn, or had no instruments to cultivate it. Or they lacked foresight of future needs. Or, lastly, they had no means of preventing others from robbing them of the fruit of their labor.

As they grew more industrious, it is natural to believe that they began to cultivate a few vegetables or roots around their huts, with sharp stones and pointed sticks. But it was long before they knew how to prepare corn, or had the implements needed to raise it in any large quantity. I should add how essential it is to husbandry to accept an immediate loss in order to reap a future gain—a precaution very foreign to the turn of a savage's mind. For, as I have said, he hardly foresees in the morning what he will need at night.

Mankind must therefore have needed the invention of the other arts to be compelled to apply themselves to agriculture. As soon as artificers were wanted to smelt and forge iron, others were needed to maintain them. The more hands were put to manufactures, the fewer were left to supply the common subsistence, though there were just as many mouths to feed. Some wanted commodities in exchange for their iron, and the rest at length found out how to make iron serve to multiply commodities. In this way the arts of husbandry and agriculture were established on the one hand, and on the other the art of working metals and multiplying their uses.

Cultivating the earth necessarily led to dividing it up. Once property was recognized, it gave rise to the first rules of justice. To secure each man his own, each had to be able to have something. Besides, as men began to look to the future and all had something to lose, everyone had reason to fear reprisals for any injury he might do to another. This origin is all the more natural because it is impossible to conceive that property comes from anything but manual labor. What else can a man add to things he did not originally create, to make them his own property? Only the husbandman's labor gives him a title to the produce of the ground he has tilled, and so a claim also to the land itself, at least till harvest. Year after year this makes a constant possession, which is easily transformed into property. When the ancients, says Grotius, gave Ceres the title of Legislatrix, and called a festival in her honor Thesmophoria, they meant that the distribution of lands had produced a new kind of right. That is to say, it had produced the right of property, which is different from the right deducible from the law of nature.

In this state of affairs, equality could have been kept up if individuals had had equal talents, and if, for example, the use of iron and the consumption of commodities had always balanced exactly. But nothing kept this balance, and it was soon upset. The strongest did the most work; the most skilful made the best use of his labor; the most ingenious found ways to lessen his labor. The husbandman needed more iron, or the smith more corn. Both labored equally, yet one gained a great deal by his work while the other could hardly support himself. So natural inequality unfolds itself gradually together with that of combination. As circumstances differ, the differences between men develop; they grow more noticeable and more lasting in their effects, and they begin to influence the lot of individuals in the same proportion.

With matters at this pitch, it is easy to imagine the rest. I shall not keep the reader with a description of how the other arts were invented one after another, how language developed, how talents were tried and put to use, how fortunes became unequal, how riches were used and abused, and all the details that go with them, which the reader can easily supply. I shall only glance at mankind in this new situation.

Behold, then, all human faculties developed, memory and imagination in full play, egoism engaged, reason active, and the mind almost at the highest point of its perfection. Behold all the natural qualities at work, and each man's rank and condition fixed. It was fixed not only by his share of property and his power to serve or injure others, but also by his wit, beauty, strength or skill, his merit or talents. Since these were the only qualities that could command respect, it soon became necessary to have them or to affect them.

Now it was in men's interest to appear what they really were not. To be and to seem became two totally different things, and from this distinction came insolent pomp and cheating trickery, with all the numerous vices that follow them. On the other hand, men who had been free and independent before were now brought, through a multiplicity of new wants, into subjection, as it were, to all nature, and particularly to one another. Each became in some degree a slave even as he became the master of other men. If they were rich, they needed the services of others; if poor, their assistance; and even a middle condition did not let them do without one another. Man must therefore now have been perpetually busy getting others to take an interest in his lot, and making them find their advantage in promoting his own, apparently at least, if not really. So he must have been sly and artful with some and imperious and cruel with others. He was under a kind of necessity to ill-use everyone he needed, when he could not frighten them into compliance and did not judge it in his interest to be useful to them. Insatiable ambition, the thirst to raise their fortunes, not so much from real want as from the desire to surpass others, filled all men with a vile propensity to injure one another. It filled them also with a secret jealousy, all the more dangerous because it wears the mask of benevolence to carry its point with greater security. In a word, rivalry and competition arose on the one hand, conflicting interests on the other, and on both sides a secret desire to profit at the expense of others. All these evils were the first effects of property, and the inseparable attendants of growing inequality.

Before signs were invented to represent riches, wealth could hardly consist in anything but lands and cattle, the only real possessions men can have. But inheritances grew so many and so large that they covered all the land and bordered on one another. Then one man could aggrandize himself only at another's expense. Meanwhile the supernumeraries had been too weak or too indolent to make such acquisitions. They had grown poor without losing anything, because, while everything changed around them, they alone stayed the same. They were obliged to take their subsistence from the rich, or to steal it. Depending on their characters, this soon bred dominion and slavery, or violence and rapine. The wealthy, for their part, had no sooner tasted the pleasure of command than they disdained all others. They used their old slaves to acquire new ones, and thought of nothing but subduing and enslaving their neighbors. They were like ravenous wolves, which, having once tasted human flesh, refuse every other food and from then on seek only men to devour.

The most powerful or the most miserable took their might or misery for a kind of right to the possessions of others, equivalent in their opinion to that of property. So the destruction of equality brought with it the most terrible disorders. The rich usurped, the poor robbed, and the unbridled passions of both stifled the cries of natural compassion and the still feeble voice of justice, and filled men with avarice, ambition and vice. The title of the strongest and that of the first occupier clashed in perpetual conflicts, which ended only in battles and bloodshed. The new-born state of society thus gave rise to a horrible state of war. Men so harassed and depraved could no longer retrace their steps or renounce the fatal acquisitions they had made. By abusing the faculties that do them honor, they labored only to their own confusion, and brought themselves to the brink of ruin.
Attonitus novitate mali, divesque miserque, Effugere optat opes; et quæ modô voverat odit.[5]

Men could not fail, in the end, to reflect on so wretched a situation and on the calamities that weighed on them. The rich, above all, must have felt how heavily a constant state of war fell on them. They paid all its costs, and although everyone risked his life in it, they alone risked their property. Besides, however plausibly they might dress up their usurpations, they knew that these rested on precarious and false titles. If others took by force what they themselves had gained by force, they would have no ground for complaint. Even those who had grown rich by their own industry could hardly rest their ownership on better claims. It was useless to say, "I built this well; I earned this plot by my labor." The answer could come: Who gave you your standing, and by what right do you demand payment from us for work we never asked you to do? Do you not know that many of your fellow creatures are starving for want of what you have in excess? Before you took for yourself more than you needed from the common subsistence, you ought to have had the express and universal consent of mankind. The rich man had no valid reasons to justify himself and not enough strength to defend himself. He could crush individuals with ease, but a band of robbers could as easily crush him, one man against all. Because of mutual jealousy, he could not join with his equals against enemies who were united by the common hope of plunder. Driven by necessity, he finally conceived the most profound plan that ever entered the mind of man. He would use the forces of those who attacked him in his own favor, turn his adversaries into allies, inspire them with different maxims, and give them other institutions, as favorable to himself as the law of nature was unfavorable.

With this aim, he first described to his neighbors the horror of a situation that armed every man against the rest, made their possessions as burdensome to them as their wants, and offered no safety either in riches or in poverty. Then he easily devised plausible arguments to bring them round to his design. "Let us join together," he said, "to protect the weak from oppression, to hold the ambitious in check, and to secure for every man what belongs to him. Let us set up rules of justice and peace, which all without exception may be bound to obey. These rules may make up in some measure for the caprices of fortune, by subjecting the powerful and the weak alike to reciprocal obligations. In a word, instead of turning our forces against ourselves, let us gather them into a supreme power that will govern us by wise laws, protect and defend all the members of the association, drive off our common enemies, and maintain eternal harmony among us."

Far fewer words than these would have been enough to impose on men so barbarous and so easily seduced. Besides, they had too many disputes among themselves to do without arbitrators, and too much ambition and avarice to go long without masters. All of them ran headlong to their chains, hoping to secure their liberty. They had just enough wit to see the advantages of political institutions, but not enough experience to foresee the dangers. Those best able to foresee the dangers were the very persons who expected to profit by them. Even the most prudent thought it not unwise to sacrifice one part of their freedom to preserve the rest, just as a wounded man has an arm cut off to save the rest of his body.

Such was, or may well have been, the origin of society and law. They put new fetters on the poor and gave new powers to the rich. They destroyed natural liberty beyond recovery, fixed forever the law of property and inequality, and turned clever usurpation into unalterable right. For the advantage of a few ambitious individuals, they subjected all mankind to perpetual labor, slavery and wretchedness. It is easy to see how the founding of one community made the founding of all the others necessary, and how the rest of mankind had to unite in turn, to stand against united forces. Societies soon multiplied and spread over the face of the earth. Hardly a corner of the world was left where a man could escape the yoke, or draw his head out from under the sword that he saw forever hanging over him by a thread. Civil right thus became the common rule among the members of each community. The law of nature kept its place only between different communities. There, under the name of the right of nations, it was modified by certain tacit conventions, so as to make commerce practicable and to serve as a substitute for natural compassion. Compassion lost almost all the influence over societies that it had over individuals. It survived only in some great cosmopolitan spirits, who break down the imaginary barriers that separate peoples, follow the example of our Sovereign Creator, and take the whole human race into their benevolence.

But the bodies politic, remaining thus in a state of nature among themselves, soon suffered the very inconveniences that had forced individuals to leave that state. Indeed, this state proved still more fatal to these great bodies than it had been to the individuals who composed them. From it arose national wars, battles, murders and reprisals, which shock nature and outrage reason. From it came all those horrible prejudices that count among the virtues the honor of shedding human blood. The most distinguished men learned to think cutting each other's throats a duty. At length men massacred their fellow creatures by thousands without even knowing why. They committed more murders in a single day's fighting, and more violent outrages in the sack of a single town, than were committed in the state of nature over the whole earth during entire ages. These were the first effects that we can see following from the division of mankind into different communities. But let us return to their institutions.

I know that some writers have given other accounts of the origin of political societies, such as the conquest of the powerful or the association of the weak. It makes no difference to my argument which of these causes we choose. Still, the one I have just laid down appears to me the most natural, for the following reasons. First, in the case of conquest, the right of conquest is no right in itself, so it could not serve as a foundation for any other. The victor and the vanquished remained in a state of war toward each other, unless the vanquished were restored to the full possession of their liberty and freely chose the victor as their chief. Until then, whatever capitulation had been made was founded on violence and therefore ipso facto void. On this hypothesis, there could have been neither a real society or body politic nor any law other than that of the strongest. Second, in the case of the association of the weak, the words strong and weak are ambiguous. In the interval between the establishment of a right of property, or prior occupancy, and that of political government, the meaning of these words is better expressed by the terms rich and poor. For before laws existed, men had no other way of subjecting their equals than by attacking their goods or by handing over some of their own goods to them. Third, the poor had nothing to lose but their freedom. It would have been utterly absurd for them to give up voluntarily the only good they still enjoyed, and to get nothing in exchange. The rich, on the other hand, had feelings, if I may so express myself, in every part of their possessions. It was therefore much easier to harm them, and more necessary for them to take precautions against harm. In short, it is more reasonable to suppose that a thing was invented by those it would serve than by those it must have harmed.

In its infancy, government had no regular and constant form. Men lacked experience and philosophy, so they saw only present inconveniences and thought of guarding against others only as they appeared. The wisest legislators strove in vain: the political state remained imperfect, because it was little more than the work of chance. It had begun badly, and although time revealed its defects and suggested remedies, the original faults were never repaired. It was patched up again and again. Yet the first task should have been to clear the site and remove all the old materials, as Lycurgus did at Sparta, if a stable and lasting edifice was to be built. At first society consisted merely of a few general conventions, which every member bound himself to observe, and the whole body stood surety to each individual for the performance of these covenants. Only experience could show how weak such a constitution was, and how easily it could be broken with impunity, since it was hard to convict men of faults when the public alone was to be witness and judge. The laws could not but be evaded in many ways. Disorders and inconveniences could not but multiply without end. At last it became necessary to entrust the dangerous charge of public authority to private persons, and to give the magistrate the care of enforcing obedience to the deliberations of the people. For to say that chiefs were chosen before the confederacy was formed, and that the administrators of the laws existed before the laws themselves, is too absurd a supposition to be taken seriously.

It would be just as unreasonable to suppose that men at first threw themselves irretrievably and unconditionally into the arms of an absolute master, and that proud, unsubdued men hit upon running headlong into slavery as the first means of securing their common safety. For why did they take superiors for themselves, if not to be defended from oppression and to have protection for their lives, liberties and properties, which are, so to speak, the constituent elements of their being? Now, in the relations between man and man, the worst that can happen is for one to find himself at the mercy of another. It would have been contrary to common sense to begin by handing over to a chief the very things they wanted his help to preserve. What equivalent could he offer them for so great a right? And if he had presumed to demand it under the pretext of defending them, would he not have received the answer recorded in the fable: "What more can the enemy do to us?" It is therefore beyond dispute, and indeed the fundamental maxim of all political right, that peoples have set up chiefs to protect their liberty, and not to enslave them. If we have a prince, said Pliny to Trajan, it is to save ourselves from having a master.

Politicians indulge in the same sophistry about the love of liberty that philosophers do about the state of nature. They judge, from what they see, of very different things that they have not seen. They attribute to man a natural propensity to servitude, because the slaves they observe bear the yoke patiently. They fail to reflect that liberty is like innocence and virtue: only those who possess them know their value, and the taste for them is lost when they are lost themselves. "I know the charms of your country," said Brasidas to a Satrap, who was comparing life at Sparta with life at Persepolis, "but you cannot know the pleasures of mine."

An unbroken horse bristles his mane, paws the ground and starts back wildly at the sight of the bridle. A horse that is properly trained puts up patiently even with whip and spur. In the same way, savage man will not bend his neck to the yoke that civilized man accepts without a murmur. He prefers the most turbulent state of liberty to the most peaceful slavery. We cannot therefore judge the natural disposition of mankind for or against slavery from the servility of nations already enslaved. We should go by the prodigious efforts of every free people to save itself from oppression. I know that enslaved peoples are forever holding forth in praise of the tranquillity they enjoy in their chains, and that they call a state of wretched servitude a state of peace: miserrimam servitutem pacem appellant.[6] But I observe the free sacrificing pleasure, peace, wealth, power and life itself to preserve that one treasure, which is so despised by those who have lost it. I see free-born animals dash their brains out against the bars of their cage, from an innate impatience of captivity. I behold numbers of naked savages, who despise European pleasures, braving hunger, fire, the sword and death to preserve nothing but their independence. Seeing all this, I feel that it is not for slaves to argue about liberty.

Some writers have derived absolute government, and all society, from paternal authority. I need not go back to the contrary arguments of Locke and Sidney. It is enough to remark, first, that nothing on earth is further from the ferocious spirit of despotism than the mildness of that authority, which looks more to the advantage of the one who obeys than of the one who commands. Second, by the law of nature the father is the child's master only as long as his help is necessary. From that time on, they are both equal, and the son is perfectly independent of the father, owing him only respect and not obedience. For gratitude is a duty that ought to be paid, but not a right that can be exacted. Instead of saying that civil society is derived from paternal authority, we ought to say rather that the latter draws its principal force from the former. No individual was ever acknowledged as the father of many until his sons and daughters remained settled around him. The father's goods, of which he is really the master, are the ties that keep his children in dependence. He may give them no share of his property, if he pleases, unless they earn it by constant deference to his will. But the subjects of an arbitrary despot are so far from having any like favor to expect from their chief that they themselves, and everything they possess, are his property, or at least are considered by him as such. So they are forced to receive as a favor the little of their own that he is pleased to leave them. When he despoils them, he does but justice, and he shows mercy in permitting them to live.

If we thus test fact by right, we shall find as little reason as truth in the voluntary establishment of tyranny. It would also be no easy matter to prove the validity of a contract that binds only one of the parties, where all the risk is on one side and none on the other, so that no one could suffer but he who bound himself. This hateful system is indeed very far, even in modern times, from being that of wise and good monarchs, and especially of the kings of France. This may be seen in several passages of their edicts, particularly in the following passage from a celebrated edict published in 1667 in the name and by order of Louis XIV.

"Let it not, therefore, be said that the Sovereign is not subject to the laws of his State; since the contrary is a true proposition of the right of nations, which flattery has sometimes attacked but good princes have always defended as the tutelary divinity of their dominions. How much more legitimate is it to say with the wise Plato, that the perfect felicity of a kingdom consists in the obedience of subjects to their prince, and of the prince to the laws, and in the laws being just and constantly directed to the public good!"[7]

I shall not stop here to inquire several things. Liberty is the noblest faculty of man. Is it not degrading our very nature, reducing ourselves to the level of the brutes, who are mere slaves of instinct, and even an affront to the Author of our being, to renounce without reserve the most precious of all His gifts? Is it not to bow to the necessity of committing all the crimes He has forbidden, merely to gratify a mad or a cruel master? Ought not this sublime craftsman to be less angered at seeing His workmanship entirely destroyed than thus dishonored? I will set aside (if my opponents please) the authority of Barbeyrac, who, following Locke, roundly declares that no man can so far sell his liberty as to submit to an arbitrary power that may use him as it likes. For, he adds, this would be to sell his own life, of which he is not master. I shall ask only what right those who were not afraid to debase themselves in this way could have to subject their posterity to the same ignominy. What right have they to renounce for their descendants those blessings that these do not owe to the liberality of their progenitors, and without which life itself must be a burden to all who are worthy of it?

Puffendorf says that we may divest ourselves of our liberty in favor of other men, just as we transfer our property from one to another by contracts and agreements. But this seems to me a very weak argument. In the first place, the property I give up becomes quite foreign to me, and I cannot suffer from the abuse of it. But it very nearly concerns me that my liberty should not be abused, and I cannot expose myself to becoming an instrument of crime without incurring the guilt of the crimes I may be compelled to commit. Besides, the right of property is only a convention of human institution, so men may dispose of what they possess as they please. But this is not the case with the essential gifts of nature, such as life and liberty, which every man is permitted to enjoy, and of which it is at least doubtful whether anyone has a right to divest himself. By giving up the one, we degrade our being; by giving up the other, we do our best to annul it. No temporal good can make up to us for the loss of either, so it would be an offense against both reason and nature to renounce them at any price whatsoever. But even if we could transfer our liberty as we do our property, there would be a great difference with regard to the children. They enjoy the father's substance only by the transmission of his right. Liberty, on the other hand, is a gift that they hold from nature as being men, and their parents have no right whatever to deprive them of it. Thus, to establish slavery, it was necessary to do violence to nature; and to perpetuate such a right, nature would have to be changed. Jurists have gravely determined that the child of a slave comes into the world a slave. In other words, they have decided that a man shall come into the world not a man.

I regard it then as certain that government did not begin with arbitrary power. Arbitrary power is the depravation of government, its extreme term, and it brings government back, finally, to the very law of the strongest, which government was originally designed to remedy. Suppose, however, that it had begun in this manner. Such power, being illegitimate in itself, could not have served as a basis for the laws of society, nor, consequently, for the inequality they instituted.

I shall not enter at present upon the investigations that still remain to be made into the nature of the fundamental compact underlying all government. I content myself with adopting the common opinion about it, and regard the establishment of the political body as a real contract between the people and the chiefs they have chosen. By this contract both parties bind themselves to observe the laws it expresses, which form the ties of their union. The people, in respect of their social relations, have concentrated all their wills in one. The several articles in which this will is explained become so many fundamental laws, binding on all the members of the State without exception. One of these articles regulates the choice and power of the magistrates appointed to watch over the execution of the rest. This power extends to everything that may maintain the constitution, without going so far as to alter it. It is accompanied by honors, to bring the laws and their administrators into respect. The ministers are also distinguished by personal prerogatives, to reward them for the cares and labor that good administration involves. The magistrate, on his side, binds himself to use the power entrusted to him only in conformity with the intention of his constituents, to maintain them all in the peaceable possession of what belongs to them, and on every occasion to prefer the public interest to his own.

Experience had not yet shown, and knowledge of the human heart had not yet enabled men to foresee, the unavoidable abuses of such a constitution. It must have appeared all the more excellent because those charged with preserving it had the most interest in it. The magistracy and its rights were based solely on the fundamental laws, so the magistrates would cease to be legitimate as soon as these laws ceased to exist. The people would no longer owe them obedience. And since it is not the magistrates but the laws that are essential to the being of a State, its members would regain the right to their natural liberty.

If we reflect on this subject with even a little attention, we shall find new arguments to confirm this truth, and we shall be convinced from the very nature of the contract that it cannot be irrevocable. Suppose there were no superior power capable of ensuring the fidelity of the contracting parties or of compelling them to perform their reciprocal engagements. Then the parties would be sole judges in their own cause, and each would always have a right to renounce the contract as soon as he found that the other had violated its terms, or that they no longer suited his convenience. It is on this principle that the right of abdication may possibly be founded. Now, if we consider here only what is human in this institution, it is certain that, if the magistrate, who has all the power in his own hands and appropriates to himself all the advantages of the contract, has none the less a right to renounce his authority, the people, who suffer for all the faults of their chief, must have a much better right to renounce their dependence. But the terrible and innumerable quarrels and disorders that would necessarily arise from so dangerous a privilege show, more than anything else, how much human governments needed a more solid basis than mere reason. They show how expedient it was for the public tranquillity that the divine will should step in to invest the sovereign authority with a sacred and inviolable character, which might deprive subjects of the fatal right of disposing of it. If the world had received no other advantages from religion, this would be enough to impose on men the duty of adopting and cultivating it, abuses and all, since it has saved more blood than fanaticism has ever spilled. But let us follow the thread of our hypothesis.

The different forms of government owe their origin to the different degrees of inequality that existed between individuals at the time of their institution. Suppose some one man stood out among them in power, virtue, riches or personal influence. He became sole magistrate, and the State took the form of monarchy. Suppose several, nearly equal in eminence, stood above the rest. They were elected jointly and formed an aristocracy. Again, among a people who had departed less from a state of nature, and whose fortunes or talents were less unequal, the supreme administration was kept in common, and a democracy was formed. In the course of time it was discovered which of these forms suited men best. Some peoples remained altogether subject to the laws; others soon came to obey their magistrates. The citizens labored to preserve their liberty; the subjects, irritated at seeing others enjoy a blessing they had lost, thought only of making slaves of their neighbors. In a word, on the one side arose riches and conquests, and on the other happiness and virtue.

In these different governments all offices were at first elective. When the influence of wealth was out of the question, preference was given to merit, which gives a natural ascendancy, and to age, which is experienced in business and deliberate in council. The Elders of the Hebrews, the Gerontes at Sparta, the Senate at Rome, and the very etymology of our word Seigneur, show how old age was once held in veneration. But the more often the choice fell upon old men, the more often elections had to be repeated, and the more of a nuisance they became. Intrigues set in, factions were formed, party feeling grew bitter, and civil wars broke out. The lives of individuals were sacrificed to the pretended happiness of the State, and at length men were on the point of falling back into their primitive anarchy. Ambitious chiefs profited by these circumstances to make their offices permanent in their own families. At the same time the people, already used to dependence, ease and the conveniences of life, and already unable to break their fetters, agreed to an increase of their slavery in order to secure their tranquillity. Thus magistrates became hereditary. They grew used to considering their offices as a family estate, and themselves as proprietors of the communities of which they were at first only the officers. They regarded their fellow-citizens as their slaves and counted them, like cattle, among their belongings. They called themselves the equals of the gods and the lords of kings.

If we follow the progress of inequality through these various revolutions, we shall find that the establishment of laws and of the right of property was its first term, the institution of magistracy the second, and the conversion of legitimate into arbitrary power the third and last. The first period authorized the condition of rich and poor; the second, that of powerful and weak; and only the third, that of master and slave, which is the last degree of inequality. It is the term at which all the rest end up once they have got so far, until the government is either entirely dissolved by new revolutions or brought back to legitimacy.

To understand this progress as necessary, we must consider not so much the motives for establishing the body politic as the forms it takes in actuality and the faults that necessarily attend it. For the flaws that make social institutions necessary are the same that make the abuse of them unavoidable. Sparta is the exception. There the laws were mainly concerned with the education of children, and Lycurgus established such morality as made laws practically needless—for laws as a rule, being weaker than the passions, restrain men without altering them. With Sparta excepted, it would not be difficult to prove that every government which scrupulously complied with the ends for which it was instituted, and guarded carefully against change and corruption, was set up unnecessarily. For a country in which no one either evaded the laws or misused magisterial power could require neither laws nor magistrates.

Political distinctions inevitably bring civil distinctions with them. Individuals soon feel the growing equality between the chiefs and the people, and it is modified in a thousand ways by passions, talents and circumstances. A magistrate could not usurp any illegitimate power without giving distinction to the creatures with whom he must share it. Besides, individuals allow themselves to be oppressed only so far as blind ambition carries them away. Looking below themselves rather than above, they come to love authority more than independence, and they submit to slavery so that they may in turn enslave others.
