It is no easy matter to bring to obedience a man who has no ambition to command; and the most adroit politician could not enslave a people whose only desire was to be independent. But inequality spreads easily among cowardly and ambitious minds, always ready to run the risks of fortune and almost indifferent whether they command or obey, according as fortune favors or opposes them. Thus there must have been a time when the eyes of the people were so dazzled that their rulers had only to say to the least of men, "Be great, you and all your posterity," and he at once appeared great in the eyes of everyone, as well as in his own. His descendants took still more upon themselves the further they stood from him. The more obscure and uncertain the cause, the greater the effect: the more idlers a family could count among its members, the more illustrious it was held to be.

If this were the place to go into details, I could readily explain how inequality of credit and authority became unavoidable among private persons, even without the intervention of government. It happened as soon as their union in a single society made them compare themselves with one another, and take account of the differences they discovered through the continual dealings every man had to have with his neighbors.[8] These differences are of several kinds. But men form an estimate of one another in society chiefly by riches, nobility or rank, power and personal merit, and I could prove that the harmony or conflict of these different forces is the surest sign of the good or bad constitution of a State. I could show that among these four kinds of inequality, personal qualities are the origin of all the others, and wealth is the one to which all the others are reduced in the end. For riches bear most directly on the prosperity of individuals and are easiest to pass from one to another, so they are used to buy every other distinction. From this observation we can judge fairly exactly how far a people has departed from its primitive constitution, and how far it has advanced toward the extreme term of corruption. I could explain how much this universal desire for reputation, honors and advancement, which inflames us all, exercises our faculties and powers and sets them in comparison; how it excites and multiplies our passions; and how, by creating universal competition and rivalry, or rather enmity, among men, it brings about numberless failures, successes and disturbances of every kind, because it makes so many aspirants run the same course. I could show that we owe the best and the worst things we possess to this desire of being talked about and this unceasing rage to distinguish ourselves: both our virtues and our vices, our science and our errors, our conquerors and our philosophers. That is to say, we owe to it a great many bad things and very few good ones. In a word, I could prove why there are a few rich and powerful men at the pinnacle of fortune and grandeur while the crowd grovels in want and obscurity. The former prize what they enjoy only so far as others are deprived of it, and they would cease to be happy, without any change in their own condition, the moment the people ceased to be wretched.

These details alone, however, would fill a considerable work. In it one could weigh the advantages and disadvantages of every kind of government as they relate to man in the state of nature. One could also demonstrate all the different aspects under which inequality has appeared up to now, or may appear in ages yet to come, according to the nature of the several governments and the changes that time must unavoidably bring about in them. We should then see the multitude oppressed from within, as a consequence of the very precautions it had taken against foreign tyranny. We should see oppression gain ground continually, without the oppressed being able to know where it would stop, or what legitimate means they had left to check its progress. We should see the rights of citizens and the freedom of nations slowly extinguished, and the complaints, protests and appeals of the weak treated as seditious murmurings. We should see statecraft confine the honor of defending the common cause to a mercenary part of the people. We should see taxes made necessary by these means, and the disheartened husbandman deserting his fields even in the midst of peace, leaving the plough to gird on the sword. We should see fatal and capricious codes of honor established; and the champions of their country sooner or later becoming its enemies, forever holding their daggers to the breasts of their fellow-citizens. The time would come when they would be heard saying to the oppressor of their country—
Pectore si fratris gladium juguloque parentis Condere me jubeas, gravidæque in viscera partu Conjugis, invitâ peragam tamen omnia dextrâ. Lucan. i, 376.

Great inequality of fortunes and conditions, a vast variety of passions and talents, and useless and pernicious arts and vain sciences would give rise to a multitude of prejudices, all equally contrary to reason, happiness and virtue. We should see the magistrates fomenting everything that might weaken men united in society by promoting dissension among them. They would foster everything that might sow in it the seeds of actual division while giving society the air of harmony, and everything that might inspire the different ranks of people with mutual hatred and distrust by setting the rights and interests of one against those of another. In this way they would strengthen the power that comprehended them all.

Out of this very disorder and these revolutions, despotism would slowly lift its hideous head. It would devour whatever remained sound and untainted in any part of the State, and in the end it would trample both the laws and the people underfoot and set itself up on the ruins of the republic. The period just before this final change would be one of trouble and calamity, but at last the monster would swallow everything. The people would have neither chiefs nor laws any longer, only tyrants. From then on virtue and morality would be out of the question. Despotism cui ex honesto nulla est spes admits no other master wherever it prevails. The moment it speaks, probity and duty lose their weight, and the only virtue slaves can still practice is blind obedience.

Inequality has reached its last term here: the extreme point that closes the circle and meets the point from which we started. All private persons return to their first equality, because they are nothing. Subjects have no law but the will of their master, and the master has no restraint but his own passions; so every notion of good and every principle of equity vanishes once more. We have a complete return to the law of the strongest, and therefore to a new state of nature. It differs from the one we started from, for that was a state of nature in its first purity, and this one is the fruit of excessive corruption. Otherwise the two states differ so little, and despotism so thoroughly dissolves the contract of government, that the despot is master only for as long as he remains the strongest. Once he can be driven out, he has no right to complain of violence. When a popular insurrection kills or deposes a Sultan, that act is as lawful as those by which he disposed, the day before, of the lives and fortunes of his subjects. Force alone upheld him, and force alone brings him down. So everything happens according to the natural order; and whatever the outcome of such frequent and hasty revolutions, no one man can complain of another's injustice, only of his own bad luck or lack of judgment.

Imagine that the reader finds again, and follows step by step, the lost and forgotten road by which man must have passed from the state of nature to the state of society. Imagine that he carefully supplies, besides the intermediate situations I have just described, those that lack of time has forced me to leave out or that my imagination has failed to suggest. He cannot help being struck by the vast distance between the two states. By following this slow succession he will find the answer to a number of problems of politics and morals that philosophers cannot settle. He will feel that men differ from one age to another, and that this is why Diogenes could not find a man: he was looking among his contemporaries for a man of an earlier period. He will see that Cato died with Rome and liberty because he did not suit the age he lived in; the greatest of men did no more than astonish a world that he would certainly have ruled, had he been born five hundred years earlier. In a word, he will explain how the soul and passions of men change their very nature without being noticed. He will see why our wants and pleasures in the end turn to new objects, and why, now that the original man has gradually vanished, society shows us only a gathering of artificial men and factitious passions. These are the work of all these new relations and have no real foundation in nature. On this subject reflection teaches us nothing that observation does not fully confirm. The savage and the civilized man differ so deeply in their hearts and inclinations that what would be the supreme happiness of one would drive the other to despair. The former breathes nothing but peace and liberty; he wishes only to live and to be free of labor; even the ataraxia of the Stoic falls far short of his profound indifference to every other object. Civilized man, by contrast, is forever on the move, sweating, toiling and racking his brains for still more laborious occupations. He keeps up his drudgery to his last moment. He even seeks death so as to put himself in a position to live, or gives up life to gain immortality. He courts men in power, whom he hates, and the wealthy, whom he despises. There is nothing he will not do to win the honor of serving them. He is not ashamed to take pride in his own meanness and their protection, and, proud of his slavery, he speaks with disdain of those who lack the honor of sharing it. What a sight the perplexing and envied labors of a European minister of State would be to a Caribbean! How many cruel deaths this indolent savage would choose rather than the horrors of such a life, which is seldom even sweetened by the pleasure of doing good! But before he could see into the motives behind all this solicitude, the words power and reputation would have to mean something to him. He would have to know that some men set a value on the opinion of the rest of the world, and can be made happy and satisfied with themselves more by the testimony of others than by their own. The source of all these differences, in reality, is this: the savage lives within himself, while social man lives always outside himself and knows how to live only in the opinion of others. He seems to receive the very consciousness of his own existence from the judgment of others about him. It is not to my present purpose to dwell on the indifference to good and evil that springs from this disposition, in spite of our many fine works on morality. Nor is it my purpose to show how, with everything reduced to appearances, there is nothing but art and mummery in honor, friendship, virtue, and often even vice, of which we at last learn the secret of boasting. Nor need I show, in short, how we are always asking others what we are and never daring to ask ourselves; and how, amid so much philosophy, humanity and civilization and such sublime codes of morality, all we have to show for ourselves is a frivolous and deceitful appearance: honor without virtue, reason without wisdom, and pleasure without happiness. It is enough that I have proved that this is by no means the original state of man, and that it is only the spirit of society, and the inequality that society produces, that transform and alter all our natural inclinations in this way.

I have endeavored to trace the origin and progress of inequality and the institution and abuse of political societies, so far as these can be deduced from the nature of man by the light of reason alone, apart from those sacred dogmas that give sovereign authority the sanction of divine right. Two things follow from this survey. First, there is hardly any inequality in the state of nature; all the inequality that now prevails draws its strength and growth from the development of our faculties and the advance of the human mind, and it finally becomes permanent and legitimate through the establishment of property and laws. Secondly, moral inequality that rests on positive right alone clashes with natural right whenever it is out of proportion to physical inequality. That distinction is enough to settle what we ought to think of the kind of inequality found in all civilized countries. For it is plainly contrary to the law of nature, however defined, that children should command old men, that fools should command wise men, and that a privileged few should gorge themselves on superfluities while the starving multitude lack the bare necessities of life.
